articles.title: Free travel pilot scheme for young people approved
articles.summary: The 29-week scheme for those aged five to 18 will run from February and is expected to cost £7.6m.
articles.body: Children and young people who live in Sheffield will get free bus and tram travel across South Yorkshire after a pilot scheme was voted through by councillors.Sheffield City Council's strategy and resources committee approved a 29-week scheme for people aged five to 18.The trial will run from 15 February 2027 and is expected to cost £7.6m.Council leader Fran Belbin said it would help families with the cost of living and give thousands of young people greater independence."The cost of a bus or tram journey should never be what stops a young person getting to college, taking up an apprenticeship, joining a sports club or simply spending time with friends," she said.Belbin revealed the pilot has deliberately been timed to run until September 2027, when a separate scheme run by South Yorkshire Mayor Oliver Coppard will provide region-wide free travel scheme for the same age group.The pilot has been developed with the South Yorkshire Mayoral Combined Authority, drawing on experience from Barnsley's MiCard scheme, which saw passenger numbers increase particularly in some of the most deprived areas.Eligible children and young people will use a dedicated smartcard and usage, journey patterns, the cost and impact on the transport network will be monitored so the success of the pilot can be assessed.

articles.title: Italian Grand Prix declared heat-hazard race
articles.summary: The Italian Grand Prix is declared a heat-hazard race as high temperatures continue in the country following the summer heatwave.
articles.body: The Italian Grand Prix has been declared a heat-hazard race as high temperatures continue in the country following the summer heatwave.A heat hazard is an official designation for an event where it is forecasted that temperatures will be more than 31C at some point during the race on Sunday.The ambient temperatures around Monza, north-east of Milan, are expected to be in the mid-30C region all weekend.They peaked at 36C on Wednesday afternoon near Milan's Linate airport.The ruling means drivers can use a system that flows cooled liquid, such as glycol, through a system of pipes in a fireproof top worn under their overalls.The cooling kit is not mandatory, but any driver who chooses not to use it has to carry 5kg of ballast in their car to ensure they do not have a competitive advantage.

articles.title: Tifo, rollercoaster or both? Osnabruck unveil new display
articles.summary: VfL Osnabruck showcase a tifo that took months to plan before their German Cup tie against Bayern Munich.
articles.body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, VfL Osnabruck have never played in the BundesligaByJude WinterBBC Sport journalistWhether it is Borussia Dortmund's famous 'Yellow Wall' or the displays that fill the stands of Bayern Munich's Allianz Arena, Germany has long perfected the art of the tifo.But second division side VfL Osnabruck have surely topped anything previously seen at a German football match by creating a tifo featuring a rollercoaster.Showcased before their 4-1 German Cup first-round defeat by Bayern Munich on Wednesday, the tifo displayed the words 'VfL Osnabruck – a rollercoaster ride!' and  a wooden cart that went along the track at the Bremer Brucke stadium.Osnabruck said the tifo symbolised its turbulent club history in a journey fans refer to as a "rollercoaster ride full of ups and downs".After "several months" of planning and building, the display also featured some of the club's major triumphs like a 1978 victory over Bayern Munich and a number of "scandals and bitter defeats".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, VfL Osnabruck currently play in Bundesliga 2The rollercoaster structure in front of the East Stand was built from wooden slats, plastic piping, fabric and was designed to be rolled out in sections.The cart, constructed primarily from wood and styrofoam, carried dummies and was repeatedly transported back to the starting point for a continuous ride through a push and pull system.The fun doesn't end there though.Osnabruck, who have recently been promoted to Bundesliga 2, said the cart passed a "photo station" where a flash went off and the "photo" of that cart instantly appeared on the right side of the grandstand.Fans even recorded a special 'Funpark Bremer Brucke' song before the match to accompany the display.The tifo was taken down just before kick-off, but the party-like atmosphere continued when Osnabruck took a shock 1-0 lead after just five minutes.Bayern, the reigning German Cup and Bundesliga champions, had to rely on two goals from England captain Harry Kane, as well as goals from Tom Bischof and Michael Olise to reach the second round.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The tifo took several months to plan and buildMore on this story

articles.title: 'Beautiful, vibrant' Disney star Carla Jeffery dies aged 33
articles.summary: Jeffery was known for playing cheerleader Bree in 2018 Disney Channel movie Zombies and two sequels.
articles.body: US actress Carla Jeffery, who was known for appearing in 2018 Disney Channel movie Zombies and two sequels, has died at the age of 33.Announcing the news, her agent Carla Alexander described her as a "beautiful, vibrant and incredibly talented woman whose radiant smile could light up any room".Jeffery played cheerleader Bree in Zombies and its follow-ups in 2020 and 2022, and previously had a recurring role in Curb Your Enthusiasm as one of the Black family, who moved in with Larry David after Hurricane Katrina.No cause of death has been given.Her management company Alexanders Talent wrote on Instagram, external: "Our hearts are broken as we mourn the loss of our beloved Carla Jeffery."For more than 20 years, Carla was part of the Alexanders Talent Management family and watching her grow from a talented young girl into the beautiful, vibrant woman and actress she became was an incredible privilege."We will remember her infectious smile, her laughter, her talent, and the beautiful light she carried everywhere she went."Our deepest love and condolences are with Carla's family and loved ones. We ask that their privacy be respected during this incredibly difficult time. Rest beautifully, Carla. You will be deeply missed and forever loved."Jeffery's twin brother Carlon, who is also an actor, reposted that statement as well as a clip of his sister on a beach and a screenshot of an undated text message."Hey Sis, call me back when you get this. I was just calling to see how your day went! I love you to the moon & back sis," it read."I just want you to know how proud I am of you. Your resilience, your grace, your infectious smile that lights up a room. You are truly a light that shines bright. Don't let anyone dim that light, even yourself."The light you carry is special and must be protected at all times. You are the best sister a brother could ask for. Pray we continue to grow closer to one another along this journey. I got your back in this life and the next."Her co-stars also paid tribute, with Chandler Kinney, who played Willa in Zombies, writing that the actress's death "doesn't feel real"."Carla. The sweetest, most sparkly gal. You made every day better and brighter with your infectious positivity," Kinney wrote."I think part of why you brought such effervescence to Bree (aside from your immense talent) is because that's really who you were in your heart; a bubbly, vivacious heart-of-gold cheerleader who loved nothing more than to uplift those around her."Milo Manheim, who played Zed, shared a series of photos with the caption: "Love you Carlaboo, the sweetest, kindest, most loving person."

articles.title: Japan halves speed limit to 30km/h on all narrow city streets
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/sep/02/japan-new-speed-limit-30kmh-narrow-city-streets
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49547763
Points: 11
# Comments: 3
articles.body: Drivers on residential roads in Japan have been forced to take their foot off the accelerator, after the speed limit was slashed from 60km/h (37mph) to 30km/h in an attempt to reduce deaths and injuries among pedestrians on narrow urban streets.The new limit, which went into effect on Tuesday, applies to residential roads with no centre line or maximum speed signs, media reports said.Narrow roads with no centre lines or pavements are a common sight in crowded Japanese cities, with data indicating that children and older people are at particular risk of being involved in a fatal or serious accident.The measures apply to about 870,000km of roads that are less than 5.5 metres wide and do not have centre lines or median strips, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. They account for about 70% of the country’s general roads, the newspaper said.Authorities hopes the restrictions will address concerns that residential areas are not experiencing the same improvements in safety seen on larger roads.While the overall number of deaths in traffic accidents is in decline – falling to a record low of 2,457 last year – those involving children and older people on residential roads has remained steady at about 300 a year since 2021, and rose for the first time in three years in 2025, according to the national police agency.The introduction in 2011 of “zone 30” areas on a limited number of residential streets and along school routes resulted in a 30% reduction in fatalities and serious injuries, the Mainichi said.Police agency data show that the mortality rate among pedestrians is less than 1% in accidents involving vehicles traveling at or below 30km/h, with the rate rising to 2.7% at speeds of 30-40km/h, and to 17.4% at 50-60km/h.“We ask drivers to recognise that they need to take particular care on roads shared by vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists,” the police agency’s commissioner general, Yoshinobu Kusunoki, told reporters this week.

articles.title: Microsoft discloses Azure revenue as part of major financial reporting changes
articles.summary:
Microsoft is changing how it reports its finances to investors by splitting its businesses into two segments and disclosing quarterly revenue for its Azure cloud business for the first time. The changes are meant to reflect the ongoing impact of AI on Microsoft and how the company now operates.
The software giant has previously reported revenue from three segments: Productivity and Business Proces
articles.body:
Microsoft is changing how it reports its finances to investors by splitting its businesses into two segments and disclosing quarterly revenue for its Azure cloud business for the first time. The changes are meant to reflect the ongoing impact of AI on Microsoft and how the company now operates.
The software giant has previously reported revenue from three segments: Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing. This is now simplifying to two: Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.
Devices and Consumer will include search and advertising revenues from LinkedIn and search advertising, as well as revenue from the Xbox division and Windows OEM and devices. Agents and Infra is essentially the rest of Microsoft, including Azure, Microsoft 365 Cloud, Microsoft 365 commercial and consumer, server products, industry solutions, and the enterprise and partner services that Microsoft now calls frontier and support services.
“There’s no question AI represents a profound shift in both technology and business,” says Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella. “It is changing what we build and how we operate, and it is blurring the boundaries between our products and reshaping our business models.”
The biggest change to this reporting structure will see Microsoft finally disclose how its Azure business is running on a quarterly basis. Microsoft has been providing year-over-year growth rates for its Azure business, reporting its Azure revenue for the first time last year. Azure revenue will no longer include GitHub cloud and other developer cloud services, nor Security Copilot and Healthcare and Life Sciences cloud revenues.
“Under this reporting structure, Azure becomes more purely our consumption-based platform and infrastructure business,” says Nadella. “Within each of these segments, you will have full transparency of quarterly revenue across each of our key businesses, including Azure, M365 Cloud, industry solutions, and ads.”
Microsoft will start using these new financial reporting changes during its first quarter fiscal 2027 earnings in late October.
articles.author: Tom Warren

articles.title: MoD withheld information about nuclear test veterans' records, ex-minister claims
articles.summary: Cold War veterans who oversaw nuclear tests have claimed they caused lifelong health problems.
articles.body: Former veterans minister Tobias Ellwood has accused the Ministry of Defence (MoD) of deliberately withholding the medical records of Cold War veterans who oversaw nuclear tests, calling it "an absolute cover-up". Ellwood told BBC Newsnight he now believes some information he gave to Parliament about the UK's nuclear programme, based on MoD briefings, was "a complete lie".Veterans have campaigned for the release of their medical histories, arguing blood and urine test results could help them prove that nuclear exposure damaged their health.An MoD spokesperson said the government had conducted an "extensive records discovery exercise" to address questions about the programme, with its findings published in full.As many as 25,000 members of the UK armed services, scientists and civilians took part in the nuclear testing programme between 1952 and 1967 at sites including Australia and several islands in the Pacific Ocean.Veterans have claimed the tests caused severe lifelong health problems, alleging they have suffered cancers of the liver, bone, bowel, skin and brain, as well as leukaemia, heart disease, stillbirths and generational birth defects as a result of their exposure.Ellwood, who served as a junior defence minister between June 2017 and July 2019, said he believed ministers over the years had been briefed to say they had no evidence to help nuclear test veterans, despite thousands of documents about the programme being held.He said the information was "deliberately withheld" by the MoD and claimed there was an effort to delay its until surviving veterans had passed away."The more you unpick this story, the more murky, the more shady, the concerning it becomes," Ellwood told Newsnight, calling it bigger than the infected blood, Windrush and Post Office scandals "because of the longevity... and the number of people that have been involved". "This is a scandal. It's absolutely tarnished the reputation of the MoD."Calling for an independent tribunal into the matter, Ellwood asked: "Why it is that the MoD - rather than help veterans, provide the information - closed ranks and said 'nothing to see here', and then told ministers such as me 'actually we haven't got that information and we're not willing to help the veterans'?"The ministry in 2024 promised to embark on a comprehensive examination of any information the department held on the issue, and has since released five reports.In those, it said there were a number of factors affecting the way medical records were kept, including the lack of a centralised approach and high levels of Cold War "secrecy". Ellwood conceded that some documents were to be handed to the National Archives, but said they would still be heavily redacted: "They have to be declassified. This isn't enough to help the veterans, who understandably remain deeply angry."An MoD spokesperson said the government had examined "tens of thousands of documents to address long-standing questions from veterans about blood and urine testing policies during the nuclear testing programme". They said it had been published in its entirety "following regular engagement between Ministers, nuclear test veterans and community groups throughout the process.""We owe an enduring debt of gratitude to the more than 22,000 Service personnel, scientists and civilians who contributed to the UK's nuclear testing programme and helped safeguard our national security," the spokesperson said.

articles.title: Argentine league to pause games this weekend to honour Messi after his retirement
articles.summary: The Argentine football league will pay tribute to Lionel Messi's international career by pausing all their domestic matches in the 10th minute this weekend.
articles.body: The Argentine league will pay tribute to Lionel Messi after his retirement from international football by pausing all of their matches in the 10th minute this weekend for a minute of applause.The 39-year-old, who wore the number 10 shirt for Argentina,  announced his retirement from the national side on Monday. The eight-time Ballon d'Or winner's final game for his country, who he captained to World Cup glory in Qatar in 2022,  was the 2026 World Cup final defeat by Spain in July."In tribute and homage to Lionel Messi's career with the Argentina national team, at the 10th minute of play in all matches the referees will stop the game and a general minute of applause will be held," the Argentine Football Association said."We look forward to seeing you on the fields - join us in this recognition!"Messi, who is Argentina's appearances record holder with 207 caps, first retired from international football in 2016 before reversing his decision.That followed a defeat by Chile in the Copa America final, in which he missed a penalty in the shootout as Argentina lost a fourth major final in nine years.The former Barcelona forward went win the World Cup and two Copa America titles with Argentina, scoring a record 125 goals.Messi made his international debut in 2005 as a 63rd-minute substitute in a 2-1 friendly win over Hungary.Having moved to Barcelona's La Masia academy as a 13-year-old, Messi has never played senior club football in his native country.He is the second-highest goalscorer in World Cup history, with 21, behind France's Kylian Mbappe (22), and second for goals in all internationals (125) behind his great rival, Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo (146).In August, he said he was considering his future in football after the death of his father, Jorge, who died aged 68 following a long illness.When he announced his retirement from international football, he said following his dad's death he was "even more convinced than before" that he was making the right decision.He will continue to play in Major League Soccer with Inter Miami, where he has a contract that runs to the end of the 2028 season.

articles.title: Here’s the first 4K 120Hz UST projector with optical lens shift
articles.summary:
A projector for people who can afford to call this a “man cave.” | Image: Awol Vision	

Detail-preserving optical lens shift is not something you expect to find on an ultra-short throw projector running Google TV, but that's exactly what you'll find inside of Awol Vision's new LuxVision. It also promises to produce an incredibly bright (6000 ISO Lumens) 4K 120Hz image measuring 120 inches when pla
articles.body:
Detail-preserving optical lens shift is not something you expect to find on an ultra-short throw projector running Google TV, but that’s exactly what you’ll find inside of Awol Vision’s new LuxVision. It also promises to produce an incredibly bright (6000 ISO Lumens) 4K 120Hz image measuring 120 inches when placed just 7.5 inches from the wall.
The vertical lens shift is the star here. Most UST projectors use digital trickery to manipulate the image onto the wall or screen behind it. The LuxVision can raise and lower the output optically to preserve the detail in the 4K image without having to move the projector or resort to keystone correction. That makes this, like all USTs, a possible TV replacement if you’ve got enough cash to offset your hatred for ugly black monoliths. LuxVision is available in a number of colors and trims for that very reason.
[Image: Customize your expensive TV replacement. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/CMF.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
Awol Vision is pitching the LuxVision at sports fans by playing up the fluidity of the 4K 120Hz display, which is still a rarity in projectors. It’s also targeting gamers by baking in Dolby Vision Gaming HDR, ALLM, VRR, and an input lag of around 1ms. You also get 3x HDMI 2.1 ports, 1x DisplayPort, and HDMI Multiview to view up to four sources simultaneously. 
As you might have guessed, these specs won’t come cheap. It’ll list for $6,499 / €5,999 / £4,999 at launch, sometime “around October.” And that’s before you shell out another $1,000 or so for an ALR screen that can dramatically enhance the viewing experience. Starting September 5th, Awol Vision is offering discounts for anyone willing to preorder the LuxVision ahead of the reviews.
articles.author: Thomas Ricker

articles.title: Belkin’s first trackers come ready to attach to your gear.
articles.summary:
Belkin’s SureFind Loop Cable Tag tracker includes a removable USB-C charging cable. | Image: Belkin	

After selling accessories for attaching Apple's AirTags to everything from keys to backpacks, Belkin is introducing its own trackers that work with either Apple's Find My or Google's Find Hub tracking networks. In addition to compatibility with Android and iOS, what differentiates these trackers f
articles.body:
After selling accessories for attaching Apple’s AirTags to everything from keys to backpacks, Belkin is introducing its own trackers that work with either Apple’s Find My or Google’s Find Hub tracking networks. In addition to compatibility with Android and iOS, what differentiates these trackers from AirTags and Google’s recently announced Pixel Tag is that you don’t need to buy any additional accessories, cases, or hardware to attach them to items. They come with lanyards or key rings already integrated into their designs.
[Image: The $15 Belkin SureFind Spot (left) and $25 SureFind Loop Cable Tag (right). https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/belkintracker2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The cheapest and simplest option is the $14.99 Belkin SureFind Spot that comes tethered to a metal key ring, but for $24.99 the SureFind Loop Cable Tag comes with extra functionality in the form of a secure carry loop that doubles as a short USB-C to USB-C charging cable. Both are expected to be available sometime this month.
[Image: The $27 Belkin SureFind Card (left) and $40 SureFind Wallet Stand (right). https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/belkintracker1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
To keep tabs on your wallet without adding a lot of extra bulk the $26.99 SureFind Card is a credit card–sized alternative that comes with an IP68 rating. It can survive a “prolonged submersion in water” according to Belkin, but since Bluetooth doesn’t work under water you’ll have to rely on the tracker’s last known location to find it.
Belkin’s most expensive tracker is its $39.99 SureFind Wallet Stand that attaches to mobile devices with magnets, functions as a fold-out stand, and protects your payment cards from wireless snooping by blocking RFID signals. While the SureFind Card is launching this month, you’ll have to wait until October for the Wallet Stand to become available.
articles.author: Andrew Liszewski

articles.title: Belkin introduces its first longer-lasting semi-solid-state power banks
articles.summary:
Belkin is joining companies like BMX, Kuxiu, and Zens with the launch of its first power banks featuring semi-solid-state battery technology. The company claims the new accessories have been "engineered to last up to 3x longer than other power banks" with the addition of a "gel-like layer" alongside the liquid electrolyte typically found in lithium-ion batteries.
Other advantages of what Belkin is
articles.body:
Belkin is joining companies like BMX, Kuxiu, and Zens with the launch of its first power banks featuring semi-solid-state battery technology. The company claims the new accessories have been “engineered to last up to 3x longer than other power banks” with the addition of a “gel-like layer” alongside the liquid electrolyte typically found in lithium-ion batteries.
Other advantages of what Belkin is calling its BoostSolid Cell technology include a reduced risk of overheating that could cause swelling or fires and consistent power delivery across a wider temperature range. They’re more expensive than power banks with comparable specs, but a longer functional lifespan should outweigh the premium pricing.
[Image: Belkin’s new semi-solid-state wireless power bank maxes out at just 15W of power delivery, and even less when charging two devices. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/belkin2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The UltraCharge Pro Slim Magnetic Power Bank 5K Qi2 15W with BoostSolid Cell is the smaller and cheaper option of Belkin’s two new power banks at $69.99. The company claims it’s 40 percent slimmer than other 5,000mAh power banks and is designed to magnetically hang on the back of compatible mobile devices and wirelessly deliver up to 15W of power. A USB-C charging port can also be used to power other devices at up to 22.5W, but charging two devices simultaneously drops the output to just 5W wirelessly and 12W with a USB-C cable.
[Image: You can charge up to three devices using Belkin’s 10,000mAh semi-solid-state power bank using two USB-C ports and a single USB-A port. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/belkin3.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The larger UltraCharge Pro Power Bank 10K 60W with BoostSolid Cell and Display offers twice the capacity with a 10,000mAh battery for an extra $20. The $89.99 power bank is also slimmer than competing options with similar capacities thanks to the increased energy density of its semi-solid-state battery tech. Power output maxes out at up to 60W when charging a single device over USB-C, but that drops when up to three devices are connected and charging using a pair of USB-C ports and a single USB-A port. And because putting screens on batteries is now en vogue, this one has a display showing charge level, power output, and the internal temperature.
articles.author: Andrew Liszewski

articles.body:
Anker’s SleepLab speaker promises to track and enhance sleep without a wearable. It uses millimeter-wave radar (60GHz) blasting from your nightstand to track micro-movements in your chest and body to continuously monitor your heart rate and breathing to enhance whatever sleep stage you’re in. It also embeds lots of hippie shit.
If I’m understanding things correctly, the speaker will — over the course of a month — determine which routines help you get the most rest, using acoustic binaural beats and lighting to gradually deepen relaxation. It operates with a touch of a button, independently of your phone, and doesn’t require a paid subscription. You can also stream audio to it via Bluetooth if you want.
[Image: “Features AI-generated persons.” https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/768px__-1.png?quality=90&strip=all]
It’s all a bit new-agey but maybe it works? It can be reserved now for $1, with the SleepLab Pro model priced at $269.99 with radar sensing, or $169.99 without. Best to wait for the reviews on this one. I’ve got a unit called in so we’ll see soon enough.
articles.author: Thomas Ricker

articles.title: Anker’s Soundcore is bringing its incredible call quality to more headphones
articles.summary:
The Soundcore Space 2 Pro will be the first headphones to run on Anker’s Thus chip. | Image: Soundcore	

After introducing the Thus processing chip in April and releasing it with the Liberty 5 Pro series earbuds, Soundcore is bringing it to more audio products. The Thus chip is behind the best call quality I've ever heard from a pair of earbuds or headphones, virtually eliminating ambient sounds f
articles.body:
After introducing the Thus processing chip in April and releasing it with the Liberty 5 Pro series earbuds, Soundcore is bringing it to more audio products. The Thus chip is behind the best call quality I’ve ever heard from a pair of earbuds or headphones, virtually eliminating ambient sounds from the speaker’s environment. At IFA 2026 in Berlin, Soundcore announced the Space 2 Pro headphones, AeroClip 2 and AeroClip 2 Pro open clip earbuds, and Liberty Buds 2.
The Space 2 Pro will be the first headphones to use the Thus chip and use a 6-microphone array for voice isolation. There are also eight microphones for the headphones’ adaptive active noise cancellation (ANC), which Soundcore claims is 1.5 times stronger than the ANC on the Space One Pro headphones across the 20Hz to 2,000Hz frequency range. (This covers the most important sound distractions including airplane drones and HVAC systems, as well as normal conversation.)
Soundcore’s latest version of its HearID listening preference test will create customized sound profiles, and the headphones support high-res audio via LDAC. Soundcore says the Space 2 Pro will get 60 hours of listening time at 50 percent volume (30 with ANC on) or 20 hours of talk time on a single charge. They launch on September 22 for $200, come in three colors — gray, white, and black — and will be available in the US, EU, and UK.
Soundcore is also expanding its clip earbuds offerings, updating the AeroClip and adding a Pro version. The AeroClip 2 looks to be similar to the AeroClip, but with the Thus chip, will retail for $170 (the same price as the original AeroClip), and come in black, red, white, and blue at launch on September 22.
The AeroClip 2 Pro will include Soundcore’s AI note-taking capability, which was also on the Liberty 5 Pro Max. But unlike the Liberty 5 Pro Max, with the AeroClip 2 Pro you can record online meetings and phone calls in addition to in-person interactions. The AeroClip 2 Pro includes a free AI transcription starter plan with 120 minutes per month for 24 months and the ability to subscribe for more transcription minutes. The 2 Pro clip earbuds use 11mm dual-diaphragm drivers, support LDAC hi-res audio, and should provide 10 hours of playback at 50 percent volume, with 30 hours total with the charging case. There’s no firm launch date or pricing yet for the 2 Pro, but we expect them later this year.
Finally, the Soundcore Liberty Buds 2 are small, 4.7-gram earbuds. They will also include the Thus chip for call clarity and use a 6-microphone ANC system. The Liberty Buds 2 will be available in purple, black, and white on September 22 for $130.
articles.author: John.Higgins

articles.title: Anker announces its first over-the-counter hearing aids
articles.summary:
Anker’s first OTC hearing aids, powered by the Thus chip, are expected in coming months. | Image: Anker	

In what could be fortuitous timing for hearing aid users, Anker announced its first over-the-counter (OTC) hearing aids at IFA 2026. It was only a couple months ago when LXE Hearing, the parent company for Eargo and Lexie Hearing - two major OTC manufacturers in the US - decided to end US oper
articles.body:
In what could be fortuitous timing for hearing aid users, Anker announced its first over-the-counter (OTC) hearing aids at IFA 2026. It was only a couple months ago when LXE Hearing, the parent company for Eargo and Lexie Hearing — two major OTC manufacturers in the US — decided to end US operations and exit the OTC hearing aid market. Now perhaps Anker can fill that void.
The receiver-in-canal (RIC) design has a main body that rests behind the ear. It uses Anker’s Thus chip, announced in April and first released in the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro earbuds series. The chip delivers the best voice isolation I’ve ever heard on any audio product and could be an incredible boon for the hearing aids.
Anker’s RIC hearing aids use four beam-forming microphones to focus on who the user is speaking to in front of them. They get up to 12 hours of use (up to 36 hours with the case) and gain two hours of use with a five-minute fast charge — Anker claims this is the quickest fast charge among its competitors.
There aren’t any additional details about exact models or US availability and pricing, but we should know more by the end of the year.
articles.author: John.Higgins

articles.title: Anker’s new printer works directly on fabrics
articles.summary: After introducing a consumer-friendly UV printer last year capable of printing designs directly on materials like wood, metal, glass, and acrylic, Anker's eufyMake brand is introducing a new machine that can print directly on fabrics. With an expected launch sometime in the spring of 2027, Anker hasn't yet revealed an official name for the new machine, but its "personal fabric printer" will offer
articles.body:
After introducing a consumer-friendly UV printer last year capable of printing designs directly on materials like wood, metal, glass, and acrylic, Anker’s eufyMake brand is introducing a new machine that can print directly on fabrics. With an expected launch sometime in the spring of 2027, Anker hasn’t yet revealed an official name for the new machine, but its “personal fabric printer” will offer multiple ways to put photos or custom designs onto T-shirts, jeans, bags, and hats.
The machine will be capable of both direct-to-garment printing where images are applied directly to soft, breathable fabrics, and direct-to-film printing where designs are first created on a film and then transferred to a wider variety of fabrics using a heat press.
[Image: Anker’s new printer is designed to replace multiple machines used to apply unique designs or images to garments. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/ankerprinter2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Anker’s personal fabric printer can apply both techniques on a single garment (although not at the same time) and can accurately reproduce colors on both light and dark fabrics. The company hasn’t revealed many details about the printer’s features and is not yet ready to talk pricing, but Anker claims the machine’s direct-to-garment capabilities will also work on embroidered designs. So instead of having to invest in an expensive multicolor embroidery machine to create colorful stitched designs, Anker’s machine can be paired with a cheaper single-color embroiderer and used to apply colors to the stitches afterwards.
articles.author: Andrew Liszewski

articles.title: Anker’s new MindBase is an AI-powered brain for your smart home
articles.summary:
The Anker MindBase offers a local solution for advanced AI processing of camera footage and is a smart home hub that supports Matter. | Image: Anker	

Anker is launching the Eufy MindBase, a local AI hub for its security cameras that runs an on-device, Anker-developed LLM, which the company says can process your footage without it ever leaving your home. It's also announcing a handful of other sma
articles.body:
Anker is launching the Eufy MindBase, a local AI hub for its security cameras that runs an on-device, Anker-developed LLM, which the company says can process your footage without it ever leaving your home. It’s also announcing a handful of other smart home security products at the IFA tech show in Berlin this week, including the TrackLight Cam S1, the S4 video doorbell, and a window camera.
Pitched as the “central brain for the home,” the MindBase is not just for Eufy security cameras; Anker is positioning it as a whole-home connectivity solution with on-device compute and local storage. Security is the first use case, but the company plans to add an energy agent for your home’s power, a clean agent for your robot vacuums, and more. Anker hasn’t revealed the price or release date yet.
Eufy got into trouble a few years back for claiming its cameras were end-to-end encrypted when they weren’t always. It has since overhauled its systems, focusing on local storage and end-to-end encryption.
Anker says the MindBase will be a Matter controller, running Matter 1.5, and will support over 40 Matter device categories, including lights, sensors, and HVAC systems. Eufy Security spokesperson Janet Jin told The Verge they plan to integrate Matter-compatible third-party cameras.
The MindBase has dual-band Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Thread, and Zigbee and will work with Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video, meaning connected cameras can work with Apple’s smart home system. It can also connect to Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and Home Assistant.
It will support 16 wireless cameras and four wired cameras, along with 34 sensors. This includes a new Smart Security Shield sensor that uses 180-degree dual radar to detect movement. Anker says it will work with a digital credential stored on household members’ phones to recognize friends and family and reduce unnecessary alerts.
With up to 48TB of expandable storage and a dedicated AI chip, the MindBase can process events directly for advanced AI features, including natural-language search across recordings and event summaries, without a monthly fee. It also supports smart alerts for facial recognition, people, car, pet, and stranger detection.
One of the first products designed to work with MindBase is the upcoming Anker Eufy TrackLight Cam S1, which will be part of an Anker MindBase Security Kit. Anker says this is an active-deterrence camera with an auto-tracking light, 180-degree dual-radar detection, and 4K resolution. Anker says Mindbase will also support a wide range of existing security cameras, such as eufyCam S4.
[Image: The Eufy S4 features a panoramic field of view. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/Video-Doorbell-S4_lifestyle-image-1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Anker’s new wired Eufy S4 video doorbell, launching this week, will be compatible with Mindbase. The S4’s other party trick is an “immersive virtual reality (VR)-inspired mobile experience,” according to the company. It shows panoramic footage in the Eufy app allowing you to look around the scene by moving your smartphone.
The S4 will cost $299.99 and features a 180-by-180 panoramic field of view, AI-powered tracking and auto-zoom, and 3K-capable recording. It has 64GB of onboard storage, supports Wi-Fi 6, uses a combination of radar and PIR for motion detection.
A $70 window camera arrives later this year. The E10 is designed for people who can’t install security cameras outside and sticks to the inside of a window to record in full-color night vision. It has on-device person and sound detection.
The company also has a new mmWave fall detection sensor. The Eufy Fall Detection Sensor (no price or release date) can be mounted on a wall or ceiling to detect falls and will automatically initiate a voice check after a detected fall or prolonged inactivity. It supports two-way communication and its self-monitoring features don’t require a subscription.
articles.author: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy

articles.title: Philips Hue adds Nanoleaf’s light panels to its ecosystem with a $40 module
articles.summary:
Nanoleaf’s colorful wall panels will work in the Hue app thanks to a partnership between the two companies. | Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge	

Philips Hue is finally adding wall panels into its smart lighting portfolio. But instead of developing its own, it's partnered with longtime rival Nanoleaf, the company that invented the smart modular wall panel category. 
Starting today, Sept
articles.body:
Philips Hue is finally adding wall panels into its smart lighting portfolio. But instead of developing its own, it’s partnered with longtime rival Nanoleaf, the company that invented the smart modular wall panel category.
Starting today, September 3rd, if you own Nanoleaf Hexagon, Triangle, or Mini Triangle wall panels, you can integrate them into your Philips Hue ecosystem using a Philips Hue x Nanoleaf Wall Light Module. The $39.99 device has a full Hue connectivity stack inside, running Bluetooth, Zigbee, and Thread concurrently — meaning you can use the Hue app and a Matter app like Apple Home simultaneously.
Once in the Hue app, the module turns the panels into a full Hue light, capable of gradient light and compatible with Hue scenes, automations, switches, and entertainment experiences. They will also integrate with the new MotionAware and Spatial Aware features on the Bridge Pro.
[Image: The Hue module is small and lightweight with no physical buttons. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/IMG_0923.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
The module snaps onto the panels the same way Nanoleaf’s controller does, but today you have to use one or the other. George Yianni, founder and head of technology at Philips Hue, tells The Verge that the option to use both modules will be coming in the next couple of months.
Until then, if you attach the Hue module, you’ll lose access to Nanoleaf’s dynamic scenes, screen mirroring, and music-reactive features. You also won’t have any physical controls for the light, something the Nanoleaf controller does offer. When dual control arrives, you can use both apps and the most recent software command will take priority, allowing you to switch between the functions of each ecosystem.
However, you can only control the Nanoleaf panels in the Hue app, not the other way around. “This is more for people wanting Nanoleaf in their Hue ecosystem than using Hue in Nanoleaf,” Nanoleaf CEO Gimmy Chu told The Verge.
Chu said he and Yianni have known each other for years and “dreamed about working together” (despite Hue’s parent company, Signify, recently suing Nanoleaf over patent infringement). Yianni said there is clear overlap in their customer base: “We often see our products installed together,” adding that wall panels have “been in our roadmap forever,” but were constantly pushed back in favor of more pressing products. ”They’re quite complicated,“ he said, and Nanoleaf had the best one out there and had “found a pretty good sweet spot” in terms of price and design. Hue could have gone more premium, said Yianni, but that would get expensive.
The two companies have been working on the integration for 18 months, choosing a collaboration over integration through Matter, because Matter doesn’t yet carry the dynamic/entertainment functionality Hue wanted. “We wanted it to behave with all of the functionality of a regular Hue product, and there’s a lot that’s not part of the standard yet,” said Yianni.
The integration is currently with the Nanoleaf Shapes products, not the Lines, Blocks, or Elements. Starting October 1, 2026, you’ll be able to buy Nanoleaf Hexagon and Triangle starter kits and extensions through www.philips-hue.com starting at $49.99.

articles.title: Three schoolgirls in Kinsale pulled up a pea plant covered in warts (2016)
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://scienceblog.com/b-three-schoolgirls-in-kinsale-pulled-up-a-pea-plant-covered-in-warts-and-instead-of-binning-it-spent-three-years-testing-13000-seeds-in-a-spare-bedroom-the-bacteria-living-in-those-warts-made-barley/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49546800
Points: 125
# Comments: 51
articles.body:
The discovery began as a suspected disease. Émer Hickey was gardening with her mother in Kinsale, on the Cork coast of Ireland, when they pulled up a pea plant and found its roots studded with pale, wart-like lumps. It looked sick. Émer, then in her early teens, did the thing that separates a science story from a compost story: she took the plant to school and asked her teacher what was wrong with it.
Nothing, was the answer. The warts were nodules, and inside them lived rhizobium, a soil bacterium in the nitrogen-fixing family called diazotrophs, which legumes like peas deliberately house in exchange for fertilizer. The bacteria pull nitrogen from the air and hand it to the plant as ammonia; the plant pays in sugar. It is one of agriculture’s oldest partnerships, and one of its most frustrating exclusions, because the world’s staple cereals, wheat, barley, rice, cannot form it.
Émer told her friends Ciara Judge and Sophie Healy-Thow, whose geography class happened to be studying the world food crisis in the shadow of the 2011 Horn of Africa famine, and the three of them landed on a question with billion-dollar aid programs attached: if cereals can’t host these bacteria, could the bacteria still help cereals?
The advice from grown-up science was discouraging. Rhizobia’s benefits were understood to belong to legumes; many people told them the bacteria would have no impact on cereal crops. The girls, aged around 14 when they started, decided the objection had never actually been tested at their scale, and set out to test it at a scale nobody expected.
Working from home, with a bedroom in the Judge house converted into a laboratory, incubation racks, hand-labeled samples, a homemade regime of controls, they soaked cereal seeds in rhizobium cultures and measured everything: time to germination, germination rate, seedling growth, dry mass. Batch after batch, season after season, for three years, they ran the experiment across barley, oats and wheat, ultimately testing some 13,000 seeds, plus thousands more in an outdoor field trial, and logging on the order of 120,000 individual measurements by hand into their notebooks and spreadsheets.
The seeds ignored the expert consensus. Treated barley and oats germinated dramatically faster and more reliably, with germination rates improved by up to 50 percent, and the head start carried through: in their growth trials the treated cereals put on substantially more dry mass, with increases running as high as 74 percent. The bacteria could not give barley a legume’s nodules, but something in the association, delivered at the seed, was waking the grain up early and sending it into the world stronger.
Irish science noticed first. The project won the BT Young Scientist of the Year in 2013, making the trio the first group of girls ever to take Ireland’s premier young-science title, then the EU Young Scientist contest. In September 2014 came the summit: at Google’s headquarters in California, “Combating the Global Food Crisis: Diazotroph Bacteria as a Cereal Crop Growth Promoter” was named grand prize winner of the Google Science Fair, beating thousands of entries worldwide. The prize haul included scholarship money and a trip to the Galápagos; Time magazine put Ciara Judge among the world’s most influential teens. They were 16 and 17, and they had started at 14, on a plant most gardeners would have thrown away.
The relevance of the result is not subtle. Germination is one of farming’s silent taxes; seeds that sprout slowly or not at all cost yield before the season begins, and a faster, more uniform start matters most exactly where the growing seasons are shortest and the margins thinnest. A seed treatment based on naturally occurring soil bacteria, needing no synthetic chemistry, is the kind of low-cost tool that travels well to smallholder agriculture, which is why the girls framed the project around food security from the first poster. They talked afterward about patents and commercialization, and the wider science has moved their direction since: engineering cereals and microbes to extend nitrogen-fixing partnerships beyond legumes is now one of agricultural research’s most funded ambitions.
The honest footnote is the usual one for prodigy science: a bedroom study, however heroically sized, is not a peer-reviewed field program, effects of “up to” 50 and 74 percent are ceilings rather than averages, and no commercial product yet traces to the Kinsale data. What stands is harder to discount. Three teenagers were told a biological door was closed, checked the literature, found that nobody had pushed on it with 13,000 seeds and three years of patience, and pushed. The pea plant’s warts turned out to be the least diseased thing in the story. The ailment was the assumption, and the cure, as it often is, was a child asking what, exactly, is wrong with this thing you were about to throw away.
articles.author: DamonHD

articles.title: Pre-Release of Polars 2.0
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://pola.rs/posts/announcing-polars-2/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49546753
Points: 363
# Comments: 120
articles.body:
Today we are releasing the first release candidate for Polars 2.0. The definite 2.0 release will land in the following weeks. We don’t aim to make a big feature release of Polars 2.0. In fact we hope it to be a boring experience for you. The reason we bump this major version is that we can get rid of design decisions made in the past that currently block us and then we want to change defaults to more sensible settings that will benefit a greater audience. The biggest default change will be that all LazyFrame queries now will run on the streaming engine. Casual Polars users can therefore expect huge improvements in memory usage and performance. In aggregate we expect the streaming engine to be easily 5x faster.
To help users transition to 2.0, we have posted a full migration guide. This post will cover a few of the highlights.
This is the biggest impact change of 2.0. Calling collect on a LazyFrame will now default to the streaming engine, leading to massive memory and performance improvements on most queries for users. The reason this required a major version bump is that the streaming engine doesn’t guarantee row-order by default for certain operations (join, group_by, unpivot, etc.). If you require observable row-order in those operations, you can opt in to that by setting maintain_order=True.
For users who want to keep using the “in-memory” engine as default, they can do so by setting the engine affinity.
lf = pl.LazyFrame({"k": [2, 1, 0], "v": ["a", "b", "c"]})
other = pl.LazyFrame({"k": [0, 1, 2], "r": ["x", "y", "z"]})
# 2.0: engine="auto" now resolves to the streaming engine.
# Row order is no longer guaranteed for joins, group_by, unpivot, ...
# │ k   ┆ v   ┆ r   │   <- order may not match `lf`'s original row order
# Opt in to observable order for this query:
# Or keep the old in-memory engine as the default, process-wide:
Polars aims to be strict and fail fast. Errors should ideally raise up-front, not 20 minutes into a pipeline. Implicit behavior on data-mismatches should be opt-in, not a default, since those mismatches can hide bugs. This strictness has become even more valuable with the rise of AI-driven development. Agents can validate a query’s structure early by calling collect_schema(), which resolves types and catches schema-level mismatches without materializing any data. This ensures fast feedback for the agents, meaning they can iterate faster. Not all errors can be caught during compilation of the query plan, some depend on data. In these cases Polars defaults to stricter behavior to ensure inconsistencies are caught instead of silently producing different results.
Below are a few examples where Polars has gotten more strict:
If you run an is_in expression on different data-types, Polars used to cast both types to their common supertype, even if that conversion was lossy
Below is an example with user-ids that can go wrong by silent data-type mismatches.
# Checking if a user ID matches a list of "flagged" account IDs
# (flagged_ids loaded from a JSON export, where large IDs became floats)
user_id = pl.Series([9007199254740993])  # Int64 -> a different ID, off by 1
Before 2.0, user_id gets coerced to Float64 to match flagged_ids. But 9007199254740993 sits above 2^53 (9007199254740992), the largest integer float64 can represent exactly, so it silently rounds down to 9007199254740992.0, giving a false positive.
In 2.0 this raises: InvalidOperationError: 'is_in' cannot check for Int64 values in List(Float64) data., users should explicitly cast to deal with lossy type conversion.
Horizontal concat will now check lengths instead of silently filling with null.
# Joining per-day transaction counts with per-day fraud-flag counts,
transactions = pl.DataFrame({"day": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], "count": [120, 98, 143, 87, 156]})
# Upstream job for day 5 failed silently
fraud_flags = pl.DataFrame({"flagged": [2, 0, 5, 1]})  # only 4 rows
│ day ┆ count ┆ flagged │
│ 1   ┆ 120   ┆ 2       │
│ 2   ┆ 98    ┆ 0       │
│ 3   ┆ 143   ┆ 5       │
│ 4   ┆ 87    ┆ 1       │
│ 5   ┆ 156   ┆ null    │  <- day 5 silently has no flag count
In 2.0 this will raise with:
ShapeError: cannot concat dataframes with different heights in 'strict' mode
If padding is what you wanted, you have to explicitly opt-in to that with how="horizontal_extend". Making that intention clear to the reader.
Removal of casts in favor of dedicated methods/constructors
Another one worth mentioning is the removal of many casts that were ambiguous or should be applied via their dedicated parsing expression, leading to one obvious way to parse data.
pl.Series([None, 1, 0, 2], dtype=pl.UInt32).cast(pl.Enum(["a", "b", "c"]))
# ComputeError: casting from u32 to enum is not supported.
Use instead: .cat.to(dtype) for int → categorical, .cat.physical() for categorical → int.
Parsing Strings to temporal data-types
# InvalidOperationError: casting from string to date is not supported.
Use instead: .str.to_date() / .str.to_datetime(). These allow you to apply a parsing format, giving you more control over how the data is parsed.
These were just a few examples, but we landed many more strictness improvements. See them all in the migration guide.
We put a lot of effort into making sure you as user or your agent can continue if you used old parameters that are not supported anymore. We added two new typed exceptions for this; polars.exceptions.AttributeRemovedError and polars.exceptions.ArgumentRemovedError that handle removed attributes and methods and removed parameters respectively.
The error messages should point you to the new API instead. Below we show two examples.
polars.exceptions.AttributeRemovedError: `melt` was removed in version 2.0;
use `LazyFrame.unpivot` instead, with `index` instead of `id_vars`
and `on` instead of `value_vars`
polars.exceptions.ArgumentRemovedError: the argument 'join_nulls' for
'DataFrame.join' was deprecated in version 1.24 and has been removed
in 2.0.0. It was renamed to 'nulls_equal' in version 2.0.
Most of the removed functionality has been deprecated for a long time and hopefully should not have affected your pipelines if you have stayed up to date. Reach out to us if you think we should have kept some functionality you relied on.
Polars 2.0 is about better defaults (most importantly the streaming engine) and a better API. We hope this release is rather boring. We don’t gate new features behind major version bumps as we ship them as soon as their ready.
Don’t be mistaken, Polars 2.x will be much better than 1.x. There is a lot in flight that we haven’t talked publicly enough: proper out-of-core support for the streaming engine, a new IO-plugin design, what we think will be the fastest S3 reader out there, major SQL coverage improvements, a cost-based planner, join reordering, and the removal of mmap, which will make our pipelines fully async end to end.
Try the release candidate by installing pip install polars==2.0rc1. Give it a spin and reach out to us here: https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/issues or contact us on discord: https://discord.gg/4UfP5cfBE7.
