articles.title: Commodore 64 released September 1, 1982
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://dfarq.homeip.net/commodore-64-released-september-1-1982/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49533497
Points: 55
# Comments: 6
articles.body: On September 1, 1982, the Commodore 64 launched. Its name referred to the amount of memory it had on board: 64 kilobytes. And it was the first computer with 64K of memory to sell for under $600.When the Commodore 64 was introduced vs when it was releasedThis is a photograph of me playing Micro League Baseball on a Commodore 64 in late December 1984 or January 1985.When the C-64 first shipped is a bit of a mystery. Commodore showed prototypes at the January 1982 Consumer Electronics Show, but these weren’t production-ready models yet. Some engineers quoted in Brian Bagnall’s books say they shipped some units in August. Michael Tomczyk’s book, The Home Computer Wars, says it launched September 1. Given that Tomczyk was writing in 1984, not long after the actual launch, I’m inclined to think Tomczyk’s date is correct. Why the discrepancy? Commodore wasn’t selling direct. So if they intended to sell any machines on September 1, they had to ship the first units in August.Commodore built the initial units in Santa Clara, Calif., but ran into quality control problems, so they outsourced production to a Japanese company called Kentron. Kentron was mass producing C-64s by January 1983.Within six months, they’d sold half a million units. And it quickly went up from there. By the end of its fiscal 1984 years, Commodore had sold about 5 million units.It became the best selling computer of all time, selling about 12.3 million units. Or, if you count the C-128 as a separate product, the C-64 alone sold about 10.6 million units.It was the computer I grew up with, and invariably, when I join a videoconference from my basement, where I have a C-64 hanging on my wall behind me, someone my age will say something about it, that they had one, or remember using one.Its early success was no accident but its staying power wasBy modern standards, it wasn’t cheap. Even in 1984, when we got one, the computer with a disk drive typically cost $450 unless you really shopped around. But the only other thing comparable both price-wise and capability-wise at the time was an Atari 800XL, and Atari was having supply chain problems in 1983, so it was a lot easier to find a Commodore 64 that year.The Commodore 64 probably would have been successful just because it was cheap and had a lot of memory for 1982. Its predecessor, the VIC-20, was the first computer to sell a million units, and it did so because it was the first computer with color to sell for less than $300. It took some weird compromises to hit that price point, with rudimentary graphics and sound capabilities and an oddball 5K of RAM.Commodore expected both the VIC-20 and C-64 to have a shelf life of around 3 years. They were about right in the case of the VIC-20, but the C-64 kept selling about 700,000 units a year through the end of the decade and was still hanging on in 1993. It wasn’t selling well in 1993, mind you, and Commodore didn’t want to be making them by then. But there was still demand for them, and Commodore in 1993 wasn’t in a position to say no to a sale.Why the C-64 had staying powerThe C-64 went through plenty of compromises to reach its price point. But they got the mix of compromises just about right. The disk drive was slower than it needed to be, largely because of a last-second design change. Its modem support was pretty limited too, but there wasn’t a lot of demand for modems yet in 1982. But it had 16-color graphics at a resolution of 160×200 or 320×200. The lower resolution mode gave you more flexibility with how you used the colors. It also had 8 sprites, which was very useful for game programming.The sound chip was a compromise. Its designer, Bob Yannes, was both an engineer and a musician. The chip he wanted to design would have been impressive for 1992, let alone 1982. He built the elements he needed, then replicated them until he ran out of room on the silicon wafer. He ran out of room at three voices, so the C-64 had three-voice sound. Some competing designs had four, but the 64’s SID chip had more flexibility with the volume of each channel, and could produce more complex sound waves than competing chips from General Instrument and Texas Instruments could.Creative programmers could coax impessive video and audio effects out of the C-64 beyond what its designers imagined in 1982. So even as the machine aged late in the decade, there was still interesting new software being released for it. By then, there were much more powerful computers on the market, but for a while that helped the C-64, as artists could develop graphical assets on one of those other computers using more powerful software, then move them to the C-64.How the Commodore 64 affected me, personallyMy story with the C-64 is a familiar one. I learned how to program it a little using Basic and 6502 assembly language. By the time I was 12, I knew how to take one apart and do simple repairs. And by the time I was a teenager, I could run a sector editor and recover data from corrupted disks, edit saved game files to make video games easier, and I will neither confirm nor deny cracking some games that used code wheels for copy protection. I knew how. I did my first writing for large audiences on a C-64 too.Everyone assumed I’d do something computer-related for a living when I got older. A lot of us did. Decades later, I run into people I knew from the local C-64 scene, and they’re working in IT like me.Jack Tramiel, the CEO of Commodore when the C-64 launched, loved hearing those kinds of stories. A Gen Xer would walk up to him, talk about how growing up with a C-64 led to a career in technology, and then Tramiel would always say something like, “And you look very successful, I’m thrilled to hear it!”I never had a chance to say that to Jack, but I did have a chance to thank one of his sons, Leonard. Leonard Tramiel was just as gracious.It wasn’t just gamesThat was the great thing about the C-64. You didn’t have to be born on third base to afford one. Yes, its price still meant it was a bit of a sacrifice for most of the 12 million people who bought one, but it was doable.The C-64 had a lot of great games, but it wasn’t just about games. I did my homework on it. Not all my teachers would accept a computer printout. But I could work out my answers, organize my thoughts, print them, and then hand-write a final draft for those teachers who insisted computers had no future.And as it turned out, computers did have a future. The job I have today did not exist in 1984. But the C-64 taught me concepts that I still use almost every day. I understand buffer overflows because of the C-64.Sometimes I return to the C-64 just to get my mind in the right place. For example, back in 2019, my then-boss told me he needed me to learn Python. I hadn’t programmed in 20 years. I’d barely even tried to program anything in 10. So I told him I’d try, but no promises. And I struggled at first. So I asked myself when I last felt comfortable programming. And I thought of the C-64. So I dug a C-64 out of storage, set it up, and started programming it in Basic, doing what I used to do, either writing simple programs, or finding an existing program and modifying it to do something slightly different. And after a few weeks of that, Python started making more sense.The Commodore 64’s LegacyI’m not the only one with C-64 nostalgia. The reason this is a retro tech blog is largely the C-64’s fault. I wrote some one-off content more than 21 years ago talking about how to set up a C-64. I figured maybe two other people in the world cared about that, but I didn’t have anything else to blog about that day, so I did it.It wasn’t long before that became most popular content. Eventually I noticed, and over time, I started writing more retro tech content, refining the formula as I went, and while demand for some other things I can write about have come and gone, demand for retro tech content remained steady or even increased. It all started with me randomly deciding to write a blog post on connecting a C-64 to a television.And the C-64 is back in production, sort of. In 2025, a Youtuber who grew up with a C-64 managed to acquire the Commodore brand and sign a deal to license an FPGA-based C-64 replacement motherboard. Starting about a year ago, the C-64 was back in production, and sold around 19,000 units at a price higher than the C-64 was selling for when it was new. Obviously it’s no longer a high-volume item so the cost per unit will be higher. But selling 19,000 C-64s in 2025, more than 30 years after the Gould/Ali-era Commodore produced its last C-64, shows the staying power this platform had.David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.

articles.title: Watch: BBC travels inside occupied Lebanon as officials say Israel expanding positions
articles.summary: The BBC's Hugo Bachega joined a UN humanitarian convoy as it travelled along Israeli-occupied southern Lebanon.
articles.body: A BBC team has joined a humanitarian mission of the UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon, known as Unifil, which is one of the only ways to visit the area under Israeli occupation.There, as it did in Gaza, Israel has flattened entire villages, and air strikes and demolitions have continued even after a ceasefire in its conflict with the armed group Hezbollah was announced in June.Western and Lebanese officials have told the BBC the Israeli military is entrenching itself in the occupied areas.Israel says it aims to create what it calls a "security zone" to prevent Hezbollah attacks on northern Israel, and that the buildings it has destroyed were used by Hezbollah for military purposes.The visit, which took place in August, was allowed by the Israeli military through a deconfliction mechanism with the UN.More on this story: Israel expanding presence in Lebanon, officials say, as BBC visits occupied areas

articles.title: Balogun has medical at Everton before abandoning move
articles.summary: Everton's move for Folarin Balogun collapses after the striker changes his mind following a medical at the club's Finch Farm training base.
articles.body: Everton's move for Folarin Balogun collapsed after the striker changed his mind over the move following a medical at the club's Finch Farm training base.Issues with the medical meant Everton and Monaco renegotiated the initial £40m deal for the 25-year-old striker. The United States international and both clubs signed a deal sheet before the transfer window closed at 23:00 BST only for Balogun to have a change of heart and walk away.Balogun had emerged as a late target after Guinea-Bissau frontman Beto completed a permanent switch to Serie A club Fiorentina.The Toffees did also explore moves for Manchester United striker Joshua Zirkzee and Aston Villa frontman Tammy Abraham, but were unable to convince either to join.Also on transfer deadline day, Everton signed Jack Grealish on a season-long loan deal from Manchester City.Grealish spent the 2025-26 season on loan with Everton, making 20 appearances, before sustaining a season-ending foot injury in January.The 30-year-old had been linked with other teams - including boyhood club Aston Villa - but has opted to reunite with David Moyes on Merseyside."I think I'm at my best at everything in life, not just football, when I feel loved. That's what the manager has given me, what my team-mates have given me and especially what the fans have given me," Grealish said."Every time I see an Everton fan, it's just pure love and the way they've welcomed me since that first game against Leeds, I'll never forget that."Grealish, who joined City from Villa for £100m in August 2021, scored twice and provided six assists in 20 appearances during his previous spell with Everton - winning the Premier League Player of the Month for August.The England international returned from injury during Manchester City's Community Shield defeat against Arsenal on 16 August.He also featured under Enzo Maresca in City's opening game of the 2026-27 Premier League season as they beat Bournemouth 2-1.Everton have also completed the signing of Ainsley Maitland-Niles from French side Lyon.The 29-year-old former Arsenal player has won five caps for England and can operate as a full-back or in midfield.Meanwhile, Scotland right-back Nathan Patterson has completed a permanent move to Serie A club Torino.Patterson, 24, joined Everton from Rangers in January 2022 and made 68 appearances across all competitions.

articles.summary:

I don't want to get too much into it, but the main reason is that my job was supposed to be leading a modernization project to expand our legacy enterprise sys
articles.body: Ask HN: How do you survive a job you hate which is slowly making you sick?36 points by _override 2 hours ago  | hide | past | favorite | 45 commentsI started a new job a little less than a year ago as a product owner/manager for a legacy enterprise system. Unfortunately the job has not at all been what I expected and what was sold to me in the interview process for a number of reasons.I don't want to get too much into it, but the main reason is that my job was supposed to be leading a modernization project to expand our legacy enterprise system with modern API-based integrations, but our development team simply does not have experience with building, testing, shipping, and maintaining APIs, which has made my job as a PO/PM considerably more difficult. Things I was used to taking a week or two max at other companies take many months to ship and aren't really built with the quality I would expect. This makes it really awkward for me when we have to meet with customers and mention that modernization and system integrations are our top priority according to the management team, yet we can't even ship a few GET endpoints after six months of work...I could go on and on, but honestly I just strongly dislike this job. I'm trying my best to find another role, but the market is really competitive right now where I live (Sweden). I would say I have a quite decent CV, with a masters from an excellent university and around a decade of work experience in tech, but Sweden currently has the third highest unemployment rate in the EU so there is a huge amount of competition for each role. But of course, all I can do is do my best.My main concern is that this job is slowly making me sick. I have started to have really concerning mental health symptoms, specifically severe anxiety, due to this job. I've also had some really dark thoughts which has scared me a lot. My doctor started me on some antidepressants and I am receiving therapy, but it's too early to say if it has helped or not.I don't know how much more I can take before I end up on some kind of sick leave. But I'm trying to take it day by day and I am trying to stay positive. Hopefully I can find another job soon, but until then I am stuck in this job.For those of you who have been stuck in jobs you strongly dislike, how did you manage to separate your work from your life so that you could survive the situation? Did you find something that worked for you to ease the situation until you could find another job?Thanks for taking the time to read this. I really appreciate any feedback or advice. help

Dell’s new Dell 14S laptop sounds a lot like a MacBook Neo: it comes in four colors, is aimed at students, and it starts with 8GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. Announced at IFA 2026, the 14S is meant to sit below the recently launched XPS 13 and offer another affordable laptop option as most other models continue to climb in price. The 14S will come in linen (beige), dusty rose (pink), washed denim (blue), and velvet green (yep, that’s green). That’s much more colorful than the XPS 13, and like its fancier brethren, the 14S can be configured with 16GB of RAM and a 512GB or 1TB SSD.
The Dell 14S isn’t as thin or as light as the XPS 13, but in addition to the same two USB-C 3.2 Gen 2 ports with DisplayPort and Power Delivery, it also has HDMI 1.4 and a 3.5mm audio jack. (Why the XPS 13 lacks a headphone jack, I’ll never understand). But the 14S has much more basic, non-touch display options: a 300-nit 1920 x 1200 / 60Hz LCD or a 450-nit 2880 x 1800 / 120Hz one. 
There are some other niceties for students on the 14S, including a 1080p webcam with Windows Hello face unlock support, and battery life that Dell claims can last for up to 23 hours of Netflix streaming. For chip offerings, it’ll be either the Intel Core 5 320 or Core 7 350 — the 14S won’t scale up to Intel Panther Lake options like the XPS 13 is soon expected to.
We don’t know how much any of this will cost just yet, as pricing is TBD for now, but in a virtual briefing Dell reps said the 14S will be close to the XPS 13’s $700 starting price yet slightly more accessible. We’ll know actual prices closer to its release later this fall. I’m currently testing and reviewing the XPS 13, and I’ve been very impressed with the hardware (except for the missing headphone jack). I’m all for seeing more good, affordable laptops out there — hopefully the 14S makes the right compromises to get the price down.

articles.title: Five moments that shaped Taylor's legendary career
articles.summary: From writing a letter to her idol as a 10-year-old to messaging a promoter on social media, here are five sliding doors moments that helped shape Katie Taylor’s career.
articles.body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Katie Taylor will fight for the final time after compiling a 25-1 professional record, becoming an undisputed world champion at two weights and winning Olympic gold and five world amateur titlesByKal SajadBBC Sport boxing journalist in DublinOn Saturday, Katie Taylor steps through the ropes at an 82,000-capacity Croke Park to face France's Flora Pili in her farewell fight.Victory on the hallowed Dublin turf would write one final fairytale chapter - a chance to bow out as undisputed light-welterweight champion and put the seal on a career that has revolutionised women's sport.There have been countless moments that have shaped the 40-year-old's journey.From a childhood letter to a Twitter direct message, these are five sliding doors moments in the making of an Irish icon.The letter to Deirdre GogartyImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ireland's first female world boxing champion Deirdre Gogarty formed a lasting relationship with Katie Taylor after the aspiring 10-year-old boxer wrote her a letterLong before Taylor became Olympic champion, she was a 10-year-old girl in Bray who simply wanted to box.There was nowhere for her to go though. Women's boxing was unsanctioned in Ireland, absent from the Olympic programme and devoid of any clear professional pathway.But there was Deirdre Gogarty. Having relocated to the United States, she became Ireland's first female professional world champion in 1997 when she defeated Bonnie Canino for the WIBF featherweight title in Louisiana."How did you do it when everyone tried to stop you?" a 10-year-old Taylor asked in a letter sent to her hero."If you keep working at it and keep showing your skills, somebody's going to say 'we've got to let this girl box'," Gogarty replied.Reflecting on the letter years later, Gogarty added: "It's mind-blowing. Especially when she wrote, 'maybe one day they'll let us box in the Olympics'."Had that letter never been written, Taylor might still have found her way to the top, but Gogarty offered hope when none seemingly existed.Heartbreak at Rio 2016 and the leap into the unknownImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Four years after winning gold at the London Olympics, Katie Taylor lost to Finland's Mira Potkonen in the Rio 2016 quarter-finalsWhen the International Olympic Committee was undecided on including women's boxing at the Games, Taylor was brought in for showcase events in front of sceptical officials in Chicago. Her dazzling displays dismantled every argument."Katie won't say this, and I've been holding back from saying this, but single-handedly, Katie Taylor got women's boxing into the Olympics," her manager Brian Peters says.Women's boxing made its Olympic debut at the London 2012 Games and Taylor claimed lightweight gold.Four years later in Rio, however, that amateur journey ended when a split-decision quarter-final defeat shattered Taylor's title defence. She was at a crossroads - rebuild for another Olympic cycle or turn professional in an era where women's pro boxing was still neglected."It was probably the worst year of my career," Taylor later admitted. "I needed a change. I needed a new mindset."Had she secured a second Olympic gold, the motivation to dive into the pro ranks might have evaporated. Instead, the sting of defeat forced reinvention.Hearn's DMs & Taylor's loyaltyImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Katie Taylor has remained with manager Brian Peters (left), trainer Ross Enamait (middle) and promoter Eddie Hearn (right) throughout her professional careerTurning professional was one thing, but securing both the right team and commercial backing was another challenge.First came manager Peters, who initially stepped in out of concern for her future."I only took her on not to see her end up with people who didn't know what they were doing," Peters says.On 4 October 2016, Taylor sent Matchroom's Eddie Hearn a direct message on Twitter, now known as X, asking if he would consider promoting her. Hearn replied 24 hours later, inviting Taylor, Peters, and her mother Bridget to a London restaurant. Hearn even borrowed his father's car to impress Taylor.The charm offensive worked and Taylor made her debut at Wembley Arena a month later.In a sport notorious for fractured relationships and bitter splits, Taylor's core team has remained the same from day one with Peters, Hearn and trainer Ross Enamait."In a business full of egos, she's stayed loyal to everyone around her and remained the most humble person you could ever meet," Peters says.Had Hearn dismissed that DM - or had Taylor lacked the enduring loyalty that kept the same tight-knit team in her corner for a decade - the promotional engine that transformed women's boxing might never have started.Image caption, Eddie Hearn shared the direct message he received from Katie Taylor in October 2016MSG & the Serrano testImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Taylor fought Amanda Serrano three times in the United States, twice at Madison Square Garden, in arguably the greatest rivalry in women's boxing historyBy April 2022, Taylor was the undisputed lightweight champion. She had already survived a razor-thin majority decision against Delfine Persoon at Madison Square Garden (MSG) three years earlier to unify - a night when many felt her aura of invincibility was almost cracked.Returning to MSG to face seven-division title winner Amanda Serrano presented a different magnitude of threat.Their blockbuster marked the first time two women headlined the storied New York venue. In front of a sellout crowd of 19,187, Taylor claimed a split-decision victory in what was widely hailed as the fight of the year.Had one scorecard leaned the other way or had the bout failed to deliver on its enormous hype, the momentum behind women's mega-fights would have stalled.Instead, the victory spawned a record-breaking rivalry. Their 2024 rematch drew global viewing figures on Netflix on the undercard of Jake Paul v Mike Tyson, before Taylor sealed the trilogy at the Garden in 2025.Taylor v PiliSaturday, 5 SeptemberCroke Park, DublinCoverage on Radio 5 Sports Extra from 19:00 BST, then 5 Live from 22:00. Ringwalks for main event expected between 22:00 and 22:30.Cameron II: Legacy on the lineImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Taylor avenged the first defeat of her professional career by beating Chantelle Cameron in their 2023 rematch in Dublin to become undisputed super-lightweight world championTaylor's first professional defeat came in May 2023 at Dublin's 3Arena when she was outpointed by Chantelle Cameron for the undisputed light-welterweight belts.At 36, questions around retirement surfaced.In the ring immediately following the defeat, Peters says he told his fighter to congratulate Cameron and ask for the rematch.Six months later, Taylor delivered a masterclass in grit, claiming a majority decision to become a two-weight undisputed champion."The pressure was immense," Peters says."For all she had done, her legacy was suddenly questioned. Had Chantelle won the rematch, who knows what would have happened?"The final pay-off - Croke ParkImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Fighting at Croke Park has long been a dream for Taylor, who has described the prospect of appearing at the iconic Dublin stadium as the pinnacle of her professional careerCroke Park is not really a sixth sliding door but rather the final pay-off.After beating Serrano in last year's trilogy decider, Taylor quietly decided she was done."She actually retired that night," Peters says. "She said, 'We convincingly beat Serrano - where do we go from there?' I said I'll agree on one condition."That condition was Croke Park or nothing."Croke Park - no disrespect to Wembley - is the greatest stadium in the world," Peters says. "You cut an Irish person and they'll bleed Croke Park."Peters insists there will be no change of heart - no Cameron trilogy and no comebacks."When Katie gives her word, that is it," he says.Regardless of Saturday's result, Taylor will be remembered as a pioneer who kicked open the door for women's boxing.More boxing from the BBC

articles.title: Children as young as six going to A&E in mental health crisis
articles.summary: NHS emergency departments are seeing more cases of self-harm, eating disorders and emotional distress in young people.
articles.body: There has been a sharp rise in children and young people - some as young as six - attending A&E units in England in a mental health crisis, NHS doctors are warning.The number of six to 17-year-olds turning up in significant distress for things like self-harm and eating disorders, or in emotional crisis, rose by 36% between 2019 and 2025, according to the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health analysis.Some faced waits of more than 12 hours once there. The college said A&Es were not the best place for them, but a lack of support in the community meant they often had nowhere else to turn. The government said it was looking to improve services and would be setting out plans soon.The analysis – based on figures provided under the Freedom of Information Act by NHS England – found there were 75,491 attendances at A&E by children and young people for a mental health concern in 2025. That is up from 55,525 in 2019 with some of the biggest rises seen in very young children aged six to nine. The increases far outstrip the overall jump in attendances, which has risen by just over 8% over the period.Doctors said the cases included children and young people brought in by families, carers and police – some of those in emotional crisis become aggressive or have challenging behaviour.In total, more than 6,200, around 8%, waited over 12 hours in A&E.RCPCH officer for mental health Dr Sam Jones said there was a lack of wider mental health care and, in particular, crisis support available in many parts of the country that meant these vulnerable children and young people were not getting the help they needed."Behind every one of these figures is a child or young person in distress and a family who didn't know where else to turn."Emergency departments are a vital safety net, but they were never designed to be a place where children in mental health crisis wait for days at time."This is a national crisis that will only get worse without urgent intervention."She said alongside greater investment in children's mental health services, staff from key agencies across health, social care and education needed better training in helping children who are struggling with their mental health.Dr Mark Buchanan, of the Royal College of Emergency Medicine, said children and young people facing a mental health crisis were ending up in A&E by "default"."They deserve care within systems and settings that are designed to meet their needs."Gemma Byrne, of the mental health charity Mind, said: "A&E can be a frightening environment for anyone in mental health crisis, let alone a child. Making them spend more than 12 hours there is simply unacceptable.She said children were not getting the support they need early enough."The current system, where many mental health services only provide support when young people are considered 'unwell enough' to qualify, clearly isn't working."She said expanding the network of young future hubs, which bring together a range of support covering mental health, employment, sports and volunteering, was a crucial step.The government is planning to publish a new mental health strategy later in the summer. But a Department of Health and Social Care spokesman said improvements were already being made with investment in mental health teams for schools and more than 150 new mental health hubs in community locations such as banks and libraries."No child should have to reach crisis point before getting the support they need," he added.Claire Evans, of Anna Freud, a mental health charity for children, young people and families, said the figures were deeply concerning."The new mental health strategy must  place children at its heart, creating the conditions for lifelong positive mental health and accelerating investment in accessible, community-based support."

articles.title: How the big five clubs strengthened their title hopes in record-breaking transfer window
articles.summary: As the transfer window closes for the summer, chief football writer Phil McNulty asks if Arsenal's rivals have done enough to challenge the champions?
articles.body: Manchester City have undergone heavy transition, from manager Pep Guardiola being replaced after 10 years by Enzo Maresca, to the departure of key figures in their glory years such as Rodri, Bernardo Silva, John Stones and Jack Grealish, as well as Savio, Omar Marmoush, Nico Gonzales, James Trafford, Nathan Ake and Tijjani Reijnders.The burning ambition remains, however, as proved by the manner in which they have attacked the market to replenish their squad for a title tilt.City paid £125m – equalling the British transfer record - to reunite former Chelsea manager Maresca with Enzo Fernandez, having already paid £116m to sign England midfielder Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest.And further quality arrived in the shape of Iliman Ndiaye from Everton for £65m, the brilliant Morocco 18-year-old Ayyoub Bouaddi, who cost £85.6m from Lille, as well as Allan Elias from Palmeiras in Brazil.It amounts to quite the rebuild, with the Fernandez deal taking City's spending to a Premier League record £458m for a single transfer window, surpassing Liverpool's £415m from last summer.However, City have also achieved around £300m worth of player sales this summer, illustrating the vast turnover at the start of the post-Guardiola era.An eventful window but one that leaves City, who still have so much class elsewhere, in good shape to mount a serious challenge.Liverpool's main task this summer after appointing Andoni Iraola to replace sacked Arne Slot, was to somehow compensate for what they would miss without Mohamed Salah after he left Anfield at the end of last season.Bradley Barcola was the prime target and eventually signed from Paris Saint-Germain for £123m. He possesses lightning pace, creativity and goals, but he is not a like-for-like replacement for Salah, preferring to operate on the left.Victor Munoz, a member of Spain's World Cup-winning squad, is another wide man who has already shown what he can deliver with a spectacular equaliser in the 2-2 draw with Nottingham Forest.Rather than simply replace Salah, Liverpool's strategy has been to find a way to get goals from the wide positions and elsewhere rather that focus on one single player to replace the Egyptian.All very well – but Liverpool's opening draws against Newcastle United and Forest showed a fault which holed them below the waterline last season has not been addressed.The lack of a natural number "6" has left a midfield imbalance that leaves them horribly vulnerable to counter-attacks. Teams can still run straight through Liverpool, but Iraola showed no inclination to make a signing in that position.Can Liverpool cure that tendency to be exposed? This could be the flaw that stops them making amends for their dismal title defence last season.

articles.title: This new Roomba seals itself to your carpet
articles.summary:
The Roomba Max 875 Combo is iRobot’s latest flagship robot vacuum mop. | Image: iRobot	

iRobot has announced a new flagship robot vacuum, which it will showcase at IFA in Berlin this week, the company's first big tech trade show in years. The Roomba maker will be exhibiting under its new owner, Picea Robotics, the contract manufacturer that purchased the once-troubled American robotics company ou
articles.body:
iRobot has announced a new flagship robot vacuum, which it will showcase at IFA in Berlin this week, the company’s first big tech trade show in years. The Roomba maker will be exhibiting under its new owner, Picea Robotics, the contract manufacturer that purchased the once-troubled American robotics company out of bankruptcy in January.
The $1,199 Roomba Max 875 Combo is the company’s newest top-of-the-line robot vacuum and mop, and it debuts alongside the $899 Roomba Plus 678 Combo. Both models are available now at irobot.com.
The key vacuuming improvement is a new sealing system iRobot is calling SealForce that takes vacuuming “to a level beyond what’s previously been possible,” iRobot chief engineer Adam Pope said.
This works by lowering a sort of skirt around the cleaning head when it detects carpet, enabling a better seal that directs airflow deeper into the carpet. Paired with a new vane-type blower motor that Pope says moves 20 L/s (liters of air per second), SealForce helps the Roomba 875 deliver three times deeper carpet cleaning than without the feature.
The 875 offers 35,000 Pa suction power, the highest iRobot has ever published—for years, the company refused to publish detailed suction-power specs. It uses a single rubber brush rather than the company’s signature dual rollers (my favorite for pet hair on carpet). Pope says this is to accommodate that better seal against the carpet. It uses lidar and camera-based vision to navigate and detect obstacles and has a slimmer footprint than the Roomba 775. It can also climb thresholds up to 3.5 cm high.
[Image: The 875 has a roller mop that can extend to the side to clean edges and a new hair-cutting anti-tangle brush. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/Roomba_Max_875_Combo_AutoWash_White_Photo_Studio_UndersideStanding_MopExtend.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The 875 Combo is also a mopping robot, with a self-cleaning roller mopping system that adds more downward pressure than the 775, plus a new heated mist feature called ThermaMist, which sprays ahead of the mop to pretreat stains. The mop includes a retractable mop cover that extends during vacuuming to keep carpets dry and can extend to get along edges. The robot comes with an auto-empty / wash dock that automatically washes the mop with hot water and dries it with hot air.
This SealForce tech is new to iRobot, but not to robot vacuums; Narwal and Dreame have variations on this on their latest flagships, the Narwal Flow 2 and Dreame X60 Max Ultra. But it is novel in the space, and combined with ThermaMist, a new hair-cutting anti-tangle main brush, and an anti-tangle side brush, the 875 shows that iRobot is inching closer to catching up with its competition than with its last relaunch.  
The company is releasing a midrange version of the 875, the Roomba Plus 678 Combo. This also has a roller mop and the new SealForce tech, but it drops to 30,000Pa suction power and 18 L/s of airflow, and there’s no ThermaMist or mop cover.
Instead, the 678 has its own treatment system called SprayForce, which sprays cleaning fluid on stains to presoak them, then comes back later. It lifts its mop 10mm when it detects carpet. Both new models work with Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and Siri Shortcuts, and are currently going through Matter certification, according to Pope.
A robot vacuum with better vacuuming is less flashy but more practical than those that sprout legs and arms. We’re seeing several manufacturers adopt this type of sealing technology — one upright vacuum makers have been trying to perfect for decades. It will be interesting to see if Roomba’s version solves that very real problem when it comes to cleaning carpet.
articles.author: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy

articles.title: Surge in horses given up by owners as costs rise
articles.summary: An Oxfordshire animal welfare charity says its Burford site is taking in 20 to 30 horses a month.
articles.body: The rising cost of caring for horses is putting more owners under financial pressure, with an animal welfare charity reporting an increase in horses being given up.The Blue Cross in Burford, Oxfordshire, says the situation has been made more difficult this year by the dry weather, leading to hay shortages and more expensive food prices.The site is currently taking in 20 to 30 horses a month, and the charity across the UK saying it has seen a "160% surge in relinquished horses in recent years".Admissions coordinator Freya Long says: "There's no grass, very little hay. I've started getting an increase in requests and I can only imagine it'll get higher with the cost of living."The charity says the costs for owners can extend well beyond feed, with veterinary care, vaccinations, worming and farrier visits all essential to a horse's welfare.Horse centre manger Vicki Alford adds: "It all adds up. We are finding, unfortunately, that people are contacting us because they can't financially look after their horses anymore."

articles.title: School uniform costs hit families, say charities
articles.summary: New government rules limit the number of branded items schools can ask students to wear.
articles.body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The government has announced new rules on the number of uniform items with school logos that students are required to wearByJosh McLaughlinSouth EastCharities in Sussex have warned new school uniform costs could add financial pressure on struggling families.This is despite new rules limiting the number of branded items state schools can require, which the government says will save parents money.Children's charity Pelican Parcels, in Brighton and Hove, said it was set to double its school uniform support by the end of 2026 in response to "rising local demand"."Every child deserves to start the school year feeling confident, with school uniform and shoes that fit properly," said head of operations Elaine Bailey. "For many families, the cost of uniform can be overwhelming."Image source, Pelican ParcelsImage caption, Pelican Parcels said it gave more than 3,400 items to school children in 2025The charity, which provides school uniforms, PE kits and supplies, said it gave more than 3,400 items to 520 children across 12 schools last year.It is seeking donations of good-quality, unbranded uniform items, including polo shirts, pinafores and PE shorts.Elsewhere, Horsham Matters, a charity in West Sussex, estimates that every school year, parents spend £336 on kitting out children for primary school, rising to £439 for secondary school.Its chief executive Kelvin Glen said: "Nobody wants to send their child into a new classroom without everything they need to learn effectively."There is copious evidence that poverty during school years has a lasting impact on children's educational attainment and life chances."What do parents think about the new rules?The government policy, which came into effect from 1 September, restricts mandatory uniform items with school logos to three for primary schools and four for secondary schools, with the latter including ties.Charlie Milner-Smith, in Worthing, said he had seen school items become more expensive with his son moving up a year at school."School shoes are definitely a lot more than they have been and kids grow out of them quickly – it's not just a one-off purchase," he said.He sees the new rules as a good thing: "It stops you having to keep up with trends and makes sure your kids can just wear more generic things."Image source, Josh McLaughlin/BBCImage caption, Charlie Milner-Smith (left) and Steph Savage (right) can see the new rules reducing their costsSteph Savage, from Surrey, can see the new rules helping with costs for her two children.She told the BBC she had just made an order, and despite already owning some uniform, spent £250. This did not include branded items."It's quite a lot to ask from parents to buy all the uniform and school-specific stuff as well – that all adds up," Savage said.Meanwhile, Lucy Smith, mother of two, said her children's school had been "quite easy-going"."If our kids walked in without any branded uniform there'd be no questions asked anyway, so it's not made much of a difference to our family," she added.In a statement from the Department for Education, a spokesperson said limiting branded items would give families breathing space and save some parents up to £50 per child.It said it was supporting schools with new guidance to take steps to bring down costs for individual items, while "keeping more money in the pockets of hardworking families".Follow BBC Sussex on Facebook, external, on X, external, and on Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.More on this storyRelated internet links

articles.title: Will new uniform rules save parents money?
articles.summary: A Fareham mum, a second-hand uniform bank and a Hampshire headteacher discuss the changes.
articles.body: A new law coming into force this school term means parents in England should have to buy fewer branded items of uniform, which the government has said will save them money.This term uniforms will be limited to three items with a school logo, like a blazer, jumper or sportswear – plus a tie for secondary schools.The government said some families would save up to £50 per child, but school wear suppliers have argued it could mean parents actually spend more in the long run.We have spoken to a Fareham mum, a second-hand uniform bank and a Hampshire headteacher about the changes.Mum-of-three Kay Devonshire-Murphy, from Fareham, said she stockpiled uniforms across the year from charity shops and second hand sales. She said having to buy three branded items was still too many."A PE top cost me £18 the other day and I had to buy three, that's massively expensive for a PE top," she said."Only three items is fine, but they're still really expensive in the places they're being sold."This year I had to buy a new blazer for my son, that was £30, a new tie. "Overall I spent £75 just for the branded stuff per child. That's a lot of money if you've got more than one child."At The Petersfield School in Hampshire there is already a uniform policy of only four items with a logo.But headteacher Mark Marande said he believed having some branded items was still important. "We have thought very carefully about which items are to be branded things like the blazer, the PE top with the house colours really helps them with their sense of belonging," he said."I think if you move away completely from branded, that would be damaging to the sense of belonging and pride the students have when coming to school." "We also recognise that on non-school uniform days attendance can dip as it can put quite a lot of pressure on students to have a particular set of trainers or a particular top or whatever that might be and uniform completely eliminates all of that."The Schoolwear Association said the plans could mean parents spend more on replacing lower-quality generic garments, which might not last as long as branded ones. A spokesperson told the BBC it could also create division in schools, because branded uniforms helped to reduce inequality and improve behaviour. According to the Department for Education (DfE), the average total cost for one child's school uniform was just under £250, based on the items required in the school year 2023/24 - with PE kit cost approximately £140.A spokesperson said the government was supporting schools to take further steps to bring down the cost of individual items.

articles.title: School opens uniform shop to sell items 'at cost'
articles.summary: The Winston Churchill School in Woking says the approach cuts £20 off the price of blazers.
articles.body: A secondary school in Surrey has secured its own uniform supplier so it can sell items at cost to pupils.The Winston Churchill School in Woking opened its own uniform shop to cut back to costs for families, where parents can order items on site or online, with clothing including skirts, ties and PE kit available at no markup from what it cost the school.Head teacher Zoe Johnson-Walker said that the approach had cut £20 off the cost of school blazers compared to the previous school year."We've been trying to reduce the cost of our uniform over a couple of years," she told the BBC.The school redesigned its uniform for 2026-27, coinciding with new government rules limiting secondary schools to three branded items, plus a branded tie.According to the Department for Education, the new rules would save parents up to £50."Parents have told us they want fewer costly branded items – and that's exactly what we're delivering," a spokesperson said."School uniform matters, but it shouldn't break the bank."Johnson-Walker said That the school had proposed removing its branded blazers from its uniform as it was "one of our most expensive items" but had found "quite a large demand from parents to sell it with the badge on"."We've managed to do a negotiation with our supplier which means that there's no additional cost to parents to have a badged item," she said.She added that the school had scrapped branded PE tops but was selling plain, black PE shirts in its uniform shop after requests from parents."We're also trying to maintain standards because uniform, as far as we're concerned, is quite levelling," Johnson-Walker added.

articles.title: BBC gains rare access to occupied Lebanon as officials say Israel expanding positions
articles.summary: A BBC team joined a humanitarian mission of the UN peacekeeping force, which says Israeli troops are fortifying positions and continuing demolitions.
articles.body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC sees Israeli military presence in southern LebanonByMiddle East correspondentReporting fromsouthern LebanonThe drive on the highway by the Mediterranean in southern Lebanon, near the border with Israel, is scenic and, these days, desolate. Crops lie abandoned and buildings destroyed by Israeli air strikes, too many to count, are in ruins.Near the town of Naqoura, a Lebanese military checkpoint, painted in the white-and-red colours of the national flag, is the last visible sign of the state's presence. Soldiers are positioned behind concrete walls, but the road is empty. A few minutes further south, around a dozen Israeli flags indicate the start of occupied territory. Unless authorised by Israel, no-one can enter.This part of the country is the heartland of Lebanon's Shia Muslim community, from which Hezbollah, the Iranian-backed militia and political party, gets most of its support. It has seen three invasions by the Israeli military in wars against the group in the last two decades alone. The most recent started in March, after Hezbollah fired rockets into Israel following the killing of the Iranian supreme leader, at the start of the US and Israel's war against Iran.Last month, a BBC team joined a humanitarian mission of the UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon, known as Unifil, which is one of the only ways to visit the area under Israeli control. There, as it did in Gaza, Israel has flattened entire villages, and air strikes and demolitions have continued even after a ceasefire was announced in June.Image source, Neha Sharma/BBCImage caption, An Israeli soldier at a checkpoint established in a residential building near the Unifil headquarters in NaqouraLed by Finnish troops who are part of Unifil, the convoy was escorting civilians to and from Christian villages near the border. Those communities were spared from Israel's attacks and invasion during the war and, with the surrounding areas now under occupation, are now cut off from the rest of the country. Our presence was allowed by the Israeli military through a deconfliction mechanism with the UN.The strip of land currently controlled by Israel constitutes around 5% of Lebanese territory and, in some places, extends 10km (six miles) from the border. Driving along the wall that separates the two countries, we saw service roads built by Israel after the invasion, intense movement of Israeli soldiers and residential buildings that were being used by them. Some were covered in netting to protect them from Hezbollah's explosive drones.We also heard Israeli surveillance drones in the sky and explosions in the distance, possibly from demolitions being carried out by Israel in villages that are under occupation.Image source, Neha Sharma/BBCImage caption, Israeli soldiers drive on a road along the wall separating Lebanon and IsraelIn a visit to occupied southern Lebanon last month, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said he had instructed the military to "take all necessary steps to prepare for a long-term presence in the area". Israeli officials say their goal is to establish what they call a "security zone" to protect communities in northern Israel from rockets and drones that have been fired by Hezbollah from southern Lebanon, as well as a possible ground invasion.According to Unifil, the Israeli military has established four new bases in the invaded areas, bringing the number of such positions to nine. Israeli forces had remained in five points after invading southern Lebanon during the previous war against Hezbollah in 2024, in violation of the deal that ended that conflict."In the past months, we've seen the consolidation and fortification of Israeli positions, construction of protective infrastructure, and other engineering works," Kandice Ardiel, a Unifil spokeswoman, said. "We have [also] observed what appear to be Israeli civilian personnel carrying out demolition and engineering activities in support of military activities in south Lebanon."Human rights groups say some of Israel's actions in southern Lebanon amount to the deliberate destruction of civilian infrastructure, a possible war crime. Hundreds of thousands of Lebanese remain displaced, without knowing when, or if, they will be able to return.In response to our questions, the Israeli military said the buildings that had been destroyed were used by Hezbollah for military purposes, and that it operated in accordance with international law. It did not respond to other specific questions about its actions in the occupied areas.Image source, Neha Sharma/BBCImage caption, Some of the houses used by the Israeli military are covered in netting to protect them from Hezbollah's explosive dronesIn June, the US and Iran announced a preliminary deal aimed at ending their conflict, which included a cessation of the violence in Lebanon. Since then, a Lebanese intelligence official told me, Lebanon's military has recorded more than 5,000 violations of the deal by Israel, including air strikes, drone attacks, shelling and near-daily incursions of Israeli soldiers into Lebanese territory beyond the area under occupation, the so-called Yellow Line.As it does in Gaza, the Israeli military justifies some of its attacks in Lebanon as operations against what it describes as immediate threats. In many cases, however, it is not clear how immediate these alleged threats are or if there is any threat at all. Hezbollah, which is considered a terrorist organisation by countries including the UK and the US, has not carried out attacks against Israel since the ceasefire came into force, but has targeted Israeli troops operating inside Lebanese territory."[The Israelis] are expanding their presence [in Lebanon]. They've [also] been setting areas ablaze, demolishing houses while the bombing continues, despite the ceasefire," the Lebanese intelligence official said. "It's clear that they don't want anyone to go back [to those villages] in the coming year, or even years. This isn't only about Hezbollah. This is about preventing people from returning."Image source, Neha Sharma/BBCImage caption, Entire villages along the border have been destroyed by IsraelIsraeli officials have conditioned a withdrawal from Lebanon on Hezbollah's disarmament, something the Lebanese government cannot deliver without the group's consent. Hezbollah, observers say, is still a significant military force despite the setbacks in the recent wars. Both countries have held direct talks that resulted in a framework agreement brokered by the US: Israel would pull out of certain areas, called "pilot zones", where Lebanese army soldiers would be deployed and Hezbollah's disarmament would be verified.Hezbollah opposes the efforts – the group's leader, Naim Qassem, called them "surrender with humiliation" last week – and says any discussion about its weapons should only happen after a full Israeli withdrawal. Israel, for its part, has claimed that the Lebanese national military, which rejects the use of force against the group saying this could pit Lebanese against Lebanese, has not done enough.The plan has seen no progress, and there is no expectation of any significant change before the Israeli election at the end of October."The idea of the 'pilot zones' seems to be dead until the context changes," a European diplomat familiar with the situation told me. "It seems we're heading to a Gaza-like situation. The Israelis are entrenching themselves... and are here to stay, for now."More on this story

articles.title: Menopausal women pose as men to buy testosterone online after prescription difficulties
articles.summary: One menopause specialist says she has seen women with up to 12 times the safe level of the hormone.
articles.body: Women are posing as men to buy testosterone from online pharmacies because of difficulties getting NHS prescriptions in Wales, according to a consultant.There has been a "very sharp increase" in testosterone referrals to the NHS for post-menopausal women, but access varies between health boards.Menopause specialist Dr Michelle Olver said she had seen women with up to 12 times the safe level of the hormone - risking permanent side effects - because they have bought online.She would like to see an equitable all-Wales approach to testosterone prescribing, with it used to help with things such as libido.The Welsh government said: "All health boards are expected to provide individualised care."While testosterone is proven to help with libido after menopause, many women also claim it helps with energy levels and cognition.Olver, a consultant in sexual and reproductive health, said it was "incredibly sad" to see women lying to get hold of the drug online, because they were being "denied access to something they need", but urged proper counselling and monitoring was needed."We want to maintain women in female physiological range for testosterone. We don't want them to have sky-high levels," she said."When you persistently have very high testosterone levels you can get undesirable permanent side effects."Nobody wants to have baldness, deepening of the voice or enlargement of the clitoris."Emma Thomas co-founded menopause support group Menopals Cardiff and Vale, and said many members had spoken of their struggles to access the hormone on the NHS."We hear a lot of women saying their GP thinks there's no need for it or their surgery won't prescribe it," she added.The 59-year-old from Sully, Vale of Glamorgan, said she noticed a shift in her own outlook at 47, when she went from a "really sociable, happy person" to someone who felt "quite insecure, paranoid, low in mood"."I'd sort of lost my joy."She felt Hormone Replacement Therapy, external (HRT) made a difference within 10 days of starting it. Once the dosage and type of HRT was stable, she was prescribed testosterone by her GP.She added it took around six months to notice an effect, saying: "It was the final piece of the puzzle for me."I feel like my old self - I've got a zest for life."Specialists and women who have tried testosterone agree it was not a "silver bullet" and would not be appropriate for everyone.Emma Jones, 57, said within a week of taking the drug she noticed her energy levels increase but also felt "jittery and on edge"."I felt like I'd changed into the body of an 18-year-old, thinking about sex from the moment I woke up," she laughed.However, Jones felt strongly that women should be able to access different types of HRT to see what works for them.BBC Wales spoke to one woman who was prescribed testosterone by her NHS GP, but when she moved to a neighbouring health board area her new GP surgery refused to continue the prescriptions.She paid for a private consultation, prescription and blood tests, but when her levels of testosterone were stable, she filled in a questionnaire for an online pharmacy pretending to be a man to get the hormone for a fraction of the cost.Olver runs the menopause clinic at Aneurin Bevan's health board and said "we have definitely seen a very sharp increase in testosterone referrals from primary care - for women wanting to access it"."It is difficult to meet demand and we have a testosterone clinic set up now for women who want to trial it."She said each of the seven health boards in Wales used a traffic light system - some are red, meaning only specialists can prescribe the drug.There are two amber options - one involves a GP requesting the support or agreement from a hospital specialist that testosterone is appropriate for a patient.The second requires the hospital specialist to start and monitor the prescription with a "shared care agreement", with GP's continuing to prescribe it."One of the main reasons for this disparity is because we don't have a licenced product for woman on the NHS," Olver said.A female testosterone product has been available in other countries for many years, and is available from private clinics across the UK.Olver said it had now achieved a licence in the UK but still needed to be appraised by NICE, external to determine if it was cost-effective to use in the NHS, at which point discussions would also be required with the pharmaceutical industry about the cost to the NHS.Currently the female product, Androfeme, costs the NHS around £100, but the male product, Testogel, is £30."Studies show about 60% of women will find benefit in improving their libido," said Olver."It's really important to manage expectations, because it's not this wonder drug that sometimes it's made out to be on social media."There's lots of reasons why women don't want to be intimate - some of those will be external factors, some will be anatomical."So it's really important to be fully counselled on what to expect when using testosterone, but also the limitations of its use."The Welsh government said: "All health boards are expected to adhere to the NICE guidelines on identification and management of menopause including providing individualised care when prescribing HRT. "We are aware this may include some practitioners prescribing testosterone for some women. "We expect all health boards to conform to any recommendation made by NICE in relation to prescribing testosterone when its guidance is published."

articles.title: Chris Mason: Will Burnham find PMQs as 'nail biting' and 'nerve wracking' as Blair did?
articles.summary: Curiously, the questions at lunchtime may well feel like a minor extension of what he faced on Tuesday, the BBC's political editor writes.
articles.body: The weekly ritual that sits at the heart of Westminster's public image beckons, the half an hour or so of verbal jousting at Prime Minister's Questions (PMQs).Prime ministerial memoirs tell the stories of how central a moment it is in the week of any occupant of 10 Downing Street.Sir Tony Blair wrote that "PMQs was the most nerve wracking, discombobulating, nail biting, bowel moving, terror inspiring, courage draining experience in my prime ministerial life, without question".Now, for the first time, it is Andy Burnham's turn to feel those nerves. And yet, curiously, the questions at lunchtime may well feel like a minor extension to the three and a half hours of questions he faced on Tuesday afternoon.And this is because Parliament is playing catch-up: six weeks into the job, Burnham is encountering the moments that would typically arrive in the opening days, the routine moments of scrutiny in the House of Commons.His arrival in office coincided with the departure of MPs from Westminster for the summer, and so the prime minister had a month or so that felt rather like a soft launch, heatwaves plentiful, Commons questions absent. Now plenty of them are coming, all at once.I observed Andy Burnham's opening moments in the Commons as prime minister from the Press Gallery. He hovered by the Speaker's chair waiting his turn, flanked by Labour's Deputy Leader, Lucy Powell, who appeared to brush some fluff from the back of his jacket, and Louise Haigh, his first secretary of state.The customary roar of approval from Labour MPs followed as he took his seat. Incidentally, MPs tend to manage this partisan and rather performative audible endorsement almost irrespective of the political weather their boss is encountering or indeed their role in creating it.But having pondered whether to stick or twist a few months back, stick with Sir Keir Starmer or twist with another card, this was their first chance to see how he – Burnham – gets on in the role.His opponents privately acknowledge his more upbeat demeanour, his sunnier disposition, is politically savvy, but they also spot laden political clouds to point at: prisons, overcrowded; defence, underfunded; social care, unreformed. A mere trio to zoom in on.The new prime minister looked at ease making an argument and articulating his political creed. But beyond a few nuggets of news – he will attend the COP climate summit later this autumn, he blames Brexit for damaging the economy, he suggested, without detail, he would find the money to crank up defence spending – we did not learn much we did not already know.His team hope this to be a pattern that becomes familiar – that ideas and plans are carefully dripped into the national conversation, taking shape and solidifying over time rather than appearing out of nowhere.They are also keen to double down on the idea that Andy Burnham is seeking to be tonally and stylistically different in how he does the job. He has posted on social media:"I want to be talking to you, the public, not just the House of Commons, so let's make it People's Major Questions rather than Prime Minister's Questions, so send me what you want to ask me and I'll answer them after the other PMQs."It is an interesting idea that it will be interesting to keep an eye on – both today and over the coming months and years.

articles.title: The Emergent Symbolic Structure of Artificial Neural Networks
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29530
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49531651
Points: 149
# Comments: 44
articles.body:
Abstract:Modern systems in artificial intelligence (AI) somehow excel in domains for which they seem poorly suited. Intelligence has traditionally been modeled as operating over structured combinations of symbols, such as logical formulas. However, the strongest modern AI systems are based on neural networks, which instead represent information in continuous vectors. Vectors seem inadequate for capturing the structure of language, logic, and other cognitive domains, yet neural networks achieve impressive performance in these areas. How do they do it? In this work, we propose a potential answer: Despite appearances, perhaps the internal representations of neural networks implicitly realize symbolic structure. In support of this hypothesis, we show that the vector representations of a variety of neural networks can be closely approximated with symbolic structures: we can replace the network's entire representation-generating process with a closed-form equation instantiating a symbolic structure, and the network's behavior remains largely unchanged. This finding holds for both small-scale neural networks trained to manipulate lists as well as large language models (LLMs) operating in four domains that are central in symbolic traditions: arithmetic, logic, computer code, and language. Further, our symbolic approximation allows us to modify an LLM's behavior in targeted ways via precise interventions on its internal representations, showing that the LLM's behavior is reliant on the symbolic structures we have identified. This work provides a potential way to reconcile longstanding symbolic conceptions of intelligence with the vector-based nature of modern AI.

articles.summary:
Article URL: https://www.lisep.org/tru
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49530989
Points: 235
# Comments: 192
articles.body: Using data compiled by the federal government’s Bureau of Labor Statistics, the True Rate of Unemployment tracks the percentage of the U.S. labor force that does not have a full-time job (35+ hours a week) but wants one, has no job, or does not earn a living wage, conservatively pegged at $26,000 (in 2025 dollars) annually before taxes.Just as an accurate census is a prerequisite to funding American communities equitably, policymakers depend on economic indicators to shape economic policy. LISEP developed the True Rate of Unemployment to provide analysts and decision-makers with a more accurate measure of Americans’ financial well-being.
