Image sourced from Good Free Photos, under CC0.The change in colour because of differences in illumination also affects its chromaticity. Consider a ‘white’ object (reflects all wavelengths of light equally) under an equal energy illuminant (emits equal energy of radiation/light for all wavelengths). The resultant spectral power distribution of this body will be a straight line — ie. equal energy across all wavelengths. Its chromaticity will lie at (0.333, 0.333) in the xy chromaticity space. Now consider the same object under the illuminant D65. The spectral power distribution of the body will now be the same as the D65 illuminant, and will lie at (0.313, 0.329) in the xy space. The chromaticity of a ‘white’ object will similarly vary for other illuminants.So a display that emits its own light, trying to mimic ‘white’ will need to take into account the illumination conditions of the environment in order to not appear out of place, and look ‘correct’. Other colours will similarly get distorted, and need to be corrected. Again, similar to how colour addition was approximated as linear, this correction can also be approximated as a simple linear transformation — by scaling the colours linearly, using the white point as a reference.Primary APrimary BPrimary CWhite point as reference The chromaticity of a colour that is being lit by the first illuminant (or how it would roughly appear, under that illuminant) is shown in black, while the chromaticity of the same colour being lit by the second illuminant is shown in gray. The chromaticity correction can be approximated by linearly transforming the colour space, such that when the colour space primaries are at their maximum intensity (or equal intensities, in the case of chromaticity), the chromaticity of the colour will be the same as the required illuminant. This acts as a reference [white] point for other colours — they are scaled using the same transformation that was used to transform the original white point to match the chromaticity of the other illuminant.True chromaticity The true chromaticity of a non-emissive object is hard to define, since it is dependent on illumination. Instead, it can be defined using its spectral reflectance, which is independent of illumination. Since an equal energy illuminant has equal energy across wavelengths, it will not distort the spectral reflectance of the object, and so the chromaticity when lit by an equal energy illuminant can be considered its ‘exact colour’.Take another look at the images of the classroom from earlier. Despite the colours being different (because of the different illuminants), they might appear similar because of chromatic adaptation. Human colour perception adjusts for differences in illumination to preserve colours of objects — by using clues from the surrounding environment. For the classroom images, the white walls may ‘feel’ white despite their chromaticity values being closer to those of yellows and blues. Other colours also can also appear ‘original’ despite being distorted by the illuminant, because of chromatic adaptation.Chromatic adaptation Notice how the whites (as well as other colours) still ‘feel’ white (or their original colour) despite having distorted chromaticities.However sometimes, chromatic adaptation can also trick the brain into perceiving wrong colours. A relatively famous, but extreme example of this is the dress. The same colours of the dress can be perceived as blue and black, or white and gold — depending on how the brain perceives the white point of the light illuminating the dress. If the brain assumes the dress is lit by a bluish light, it tries to correct for it, making the dress look white and gold. Conversely, if the brain assumes a warmer illuminant, the brain tries correcting the colour distortion, making the dress appear blue and black.Chromatic adaptation: Blue and black dress The above graphic shows how the colours of a blue and black dress would look if it is distorted by a yellowish illuminant. If the brain assumes the illuminant is indeed yellowish, it would try to ‘correct’ the colours to their ‘original’ hues, which in this case would be blue and black. Image sourced Tumblr (archived), under fair use.Chromatic adaptation: White and gold dress Similarly here, how the colours of a white and gold dress might get distorted by a bluish illuminant is shown above. The brain, assuming the illuminant is tinted blue, would try to correct the colours back to white and gold. Notice that the colours of the right image in both the above and below graphic are the exact same. But how the colours are perceived by the brain depends on whether it assumed a warm or cool illuminant. In very ambiguous cases like these, it might be equally likely for people to perceive it as either of the two.The above scenario is an example of what happens when colours are quantified without correcting for the white point (illumination) — it can look out of place, and in extreme cases like the dress, even lead to completely wrong colour description and reproduction. If the colours of the dress are mapped on the chromaticity diagram directly without any corrections, it will not always describe the ‘real’ chromaticity of the dress.For example, here, the colours of two pixels with blue/white and black/gold are mapped on the xy chromaticity diagram. Notice how the chromaticity values correspond to bluish and yellowish hues, suggesting the colours are actually blue and gold. This is obviously not the case. The colours can be corrected by changing the white point, by applying the same linear white point transformation from above.Chromaticity of the dress colours The chromaticity of the dress on the xy chromaticity diagram maps to values that correspond to (somewhat) bluish and yellowish chromaticities. But the actual colours of the dress are blue and black. Setting the white point to a warmer colour and then transforming it to the equal energy illuminant would transform the chromaticity values to result in more accurate approximations of the ‘true’ colours of the dress.For accurate colour quantification and reproduction, the illumination of the environment needs to be taken into account too — when quantifying colours of non-emissive objects, which are most of objects around us.Colour ScienceThe original questions should be easy to answer now. Colour blindness exists because of cone anomalies. Addition of colours results in a colour whose brightness (luminance) is the sum of the luminance of the colourants, and its hue or chromaticity is the ratios of its colourants. The multiplication of colours can be thought of as a colour reflecting the colour of another coloured illuminant. Colour hexcodes, even with 16,777,216 possible values, are still limited by their primaries. And the dress appears both white and gold, and blue and black because of chromatic adaptation.Colours are a very interesting topic, because it involves quantifying something that feels innately qualitative. This article mainly discusses additive colour models, but subtractive and other colour models are just as interesting. Most of these topics involve ways to describe and recreate colours. But there are also entirely different branch of science that deal with the psychology of colours — why certain colour combinations appear pleasing, how the meaning of colours vary across cultures, or how colours affect other senses.The subject of colours is vast — spanning scientific domains from quantum physics and electromagnetism to physiology and psychology. This post is a very tiny fraction of what constitutes colour science.ReferencesJamie Wong: Color: From Hexcodes to EyeballsBartosz Ciechanowski: Color SpacesDouglas A. Kerr: The CIE XYZ and xyY Color Spaces

articles.title: Christian festival 'devastated' as man dies after sign falls
articles.summary: Police say at least six other people were also injured in the incident at the Big Church Festival.
articles.body: Organisers of a Christian festival say they are "devastated" after a man died and six other people were injured by a falling sign.Sussex Police said it had been called to the Big Church Festival at Wiston Park, near Steyning in West Sussex, at about 15:38 BST on Friday.It was later confirmed a 41-year-old man from Eastbourne in East Sussex had died.The Archbishop of Canterbury said she was "sad and shocked" to hear about the fatal incident.Dame Sarah Mullally said: "I pray for his family, friends and loved ones as they grieve. I pray for those receiving treatment, and the healthcare workers looking after them."And I pray too for the other festival goers, staff and event organisers as they come to terms with these tragic events. "May the God of comfort and healing be with them all."South East Coast Ambulance service said four of the six people injured were taken to local hospitals for further treatment, with two people having serious injuries.The Big Church Festival, which describes itself as the UK's biggest Christian festival, was founded in 2009.The festival began on Friday and was due to continue until Sunday, but a decision was made by organisers to cancel the remainder of the event after the incident."We are working with the emergency services, police and the Health and Safety Executive as they establish the circumstances surrounding today's incident," the organisers said."We are incredibly grateful to everyone who responded, and to our teams and community for the care they have shown one another."

articles.title: The Theragun Sense makes everyday recovery surprisingly easy
articles.summary: The Theragun Sense, which retails for $299, is a wellness-focused massage gun that’s designed for everyday aches, muscle tension, relaxation, and soreness.
articles.body:
As my 20s are set to come to an end later this year, I’ve officially reached the age where sleeping in the wrong position or stretching just a little too far can cause aches and pains. I’ve always been somewhat skeptical of massage guns, mostly because I’ve tried a few off-brand ones and just assumed they’d eventually end up collecting dust in a drawer.
But after a few weeks of testing the Therabody Theragun Sense (2nd Gen), I was surprised. Turns out massage guns aren’t as gimmicky as I had thought.
The Theragun Sense, which retails for $299, is a wellness-focused massage gun that’s designed for everyday aches, muscle tension, relaxation, and soreness. It’s more of a gentle massaging and relaxation tool rather than a hardcore recovery massage gun.
If you’re looking for more of a deep-tissue massage, it might be worth checking out the Theragun PRO or Prime. But if you don’t need a super heavy-duty massage gun with features like heated therapy and deep- tissue capabilities, the Theragun Sense is a great option for everyday use.
My favorite thing about the massage gun is that it features built-in visually guided routines. The device comes with four routines, and you can access additional routines through the Therabody app and sync your favorite ones to the device using Bluetooth.
The Theragun Sense has an LCD screen that walks you through routines step by step. Once you select a routine, the screen shows you exactly where to use the massage gun, how long to spend on each area, and how much pressure to apply.
As someone who never really had an idea of what to do with a massage gun other than pointing it to a sore muscle and hoping for the best, I liked that the Therabody Sense takes a lot of the guesswork out of using a massage gun.
My favorite routine was the six-minute “Sleep” routine that’s essentially a quick full-body massage to get you ready for the night. The app lets you choose from many other routines, like “Pre-Walk Warm-up,” “Desk Relief,” “Lower Back Recovery,” and more.
The massage gun features five speeds to fine-tune pressure to allow for a more relaxing touch, moderate pressure, or a deeper tension release. I liked having the flexibility to change the intensity depending on how sore I was feeling that day.
Since the device is designed to be lightweight, I found it easy to hold and get to those spots on my back and shoulders that are harder to reach.
For people who want more personalization, the Therabody app takes the guided experience a step further with Coach, the company’s AI feature that creates personalized recovery recommendations based on your goals and activity. Coach can recommend which part of your body to target, which settings or attachments to use, and when to fit a recovery session into your day.
The relatively quiet motor was another feature I appreciated, as I could easily use the device while watching TV or relaxing without the sound of the massage gun acting as a distraction.
The Theragun Sense comes with a USB-C charging cable, a travel pouch, and two massage attachments: the Standard Ball and the Dampener, which is designed to target knots and tender areas. Separately, you can purchase the “Supersoft” attachment for $35 for extra sensitive areas on the body.
Overall, the Theragun Sense (2nd Gen) won me over. It’s easy to use, comfortable to hold, and notably takes the guesswork out of using a massage gun. At $299, it isn’t cheap, but I think it’s a great option for people who want an everyday wellness device that can help them relax and recover.

articles.title: Nvidia’s AI advantage is moving beyond the GPU
articles.summary: The new generation of data center systems is increasing efficiency with smarter traffic control instead of just more processor cycles.
articles.body:
Before this week, the dominant story about Nvidia went something like this: For the first few years of the AI boom, Nvidia was the only source for state-of-the-art GPUs, which became immensely profitable as the industry scaled out. In the last few years, hyperscalers like Amazon and Google have started building their own chips, and Nvidia is no longer the only game in town, leading many investors to wonder how durable its advantage really is.
It’s a compelling story, and mostly true. After growing its market cap 10x between the start of 2023 and mid-2025, Nvidia shares have been on a more modest trajectory for the past year, driven by concerns about GPU competition.
A new narrative has taken shape since the company’s earnings on Wednesday and investors are starting to realize that Nvidia’s advantage goes far beyond GPUs. As AI’s compute grows into the gigawatt scale, orchestration has become an increasingly complex task. Not surprisingly, Nvidia has built much of the state-of-the-art hardware needed to handle it, giving the company a huge advantage in the systems that surround the GPU even as it sees increased competition on the GPUs themselves.
For all the talk of compute as a commodity, it’s still incredibly difficult to operate a megascale data center at peak efficiency — and as deployments get bigger and faster, that challenge is only growing.
You can see some of this just by looking at the details of what Nvidia is actually selling. The company is currently rolling out its Vera Rubin architecture, which pairs the Rubin GPU with a collection of other units, including the Vera CPU, the Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator and similar racks for storage and networking.
Over the past week, I’ve been talking to folks at Nvidia about what those systems actually do, and the results have been surprising. Like the Rubin GPU itself, they’re extremely specialized systems, but instead of churning through tokens, they’re making sure everything outside the GPU works as efficiently as possible. If the GPU is the engine, these are the rest of the car.
The Vera CPU in particular is focused on the problem of orchestrating data. “Vera is important because there’s only so much memory that you can put in a single server or any sort of compute platform,” Jason Hardy, Nvidia’s VP of storage technology, told me.
As data centers have scaled up computing power, memory capacity has scaled up too, which is why companies like Micron have gotten rich in the second wave of the infrastructure boom. But getting that data to the GPU at the right time isn’t straightforward — and as companies look to drive tokens-per-watt lower and lower, they’re realizing how important that kind of traffic direction is.
“We saw upwards of 3x improvement in these operations, where the Vera CPU is allowing for acceleration,” Hardy said. “So now we can use our flash to its fullest potential, because we can get all that performance out of it without bottlenecking.”
You can see versions of the same problem outside of Nvidia. When OpenAI developed its Jalapeño chip, a major focus was avoiding these challenges entirely by minimizing the amount of data that needs to be moved around.
“We designed Jalapeño to minimize data movement and communication delays,” the company said in a blog post earlier this month. “Its large domain allows the entire workload to remain within one connected system, minimizing data movement and helping the complete request stay fast and efficient from beginning to end.”
It’s a different approach, avoiding data movement entirely by conducting a workload within one integrated chip. But the overall logic is the same, increasing efficiency with smarter traffic control instead of just more processor cycles. That in turn opens up a whole new layer of infrastructure for companies to compete over.
This new focus on data orchestration isn’t automatically a win for Nvidia. The company will have to compete with rival chipmakers and hyperscalers just as it has with GPUs. But the competition has moved to a new layer, where building a rival GPU matters less than being able to make the entire system work efficiently.
And at least in the early stages, Nvidia looks to have a commanding lead.

articles.title: The Galaxy Z Flip 8 is at its best when there’s friction
articles.summary:
The Z Flip 8 is designed to be used shut more than ever before. | Photo: Dominic Preston / The Verge	

What do you want from a flip phone when it's closed? A simple interface, perhaps notifications and a widget or two, for handling the basics? Or a fully fledged Android experience shrunk down for the Flip form factor? For years, Samsung has insisted on the former, even as some fans - and Razr riva
articles.body:
What do you want from a flip phone when it’s closed? A simple interface, perhaps notifications and a widget or two, for handling the basics? Or a fully fledged Android experience shrunk down for the Flip form factor? For years, Samsung has insisted on the former, even as some fans — and Razr rival Motorola — have pushed for the latter. With the Galaxy Z Flip 8, Samsung has given in.
Although the Z Flip 8’s hardware is almost unchanged year-on-year, Samsung has fundamentally rethought how this phone is meant to be used when shut. The cover screen feels more like a regular Android phone, with easier access to the full versions of every single app, letting you browse social media, watch movies, and play games without ever opening the phone. Not every app works well on a tiny square screen with two cameras in the middle of it, but even when they don’t, that friction between me and the distractions of my phone still feels as much a feature as a bug.
[Product: Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8 | https://www.amazon.com/Samsung-Galaxy-Flip8-Unlocked-Graphite/dp/B0H12FP315/?tag=theverge02-20, https://go.skimresources.com/?id=1025X1701640&xs=1&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.samsung.com%2Fus%2Fsmartphones%2Fgalaxy-z-flip8%2Fbuy%2F, https://bestbuy.7tiv.net/c/482924/614286/10014?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bestbuy.com%2Fproduct%2Fsamsung-galaxy-z-flip8-256gb-unlocked-graphite%2FJJGRF3TF7P]
Everything exciting about the Z Flip 8 lies in its 4-inch cover screen, which is now more versatile than ever thanks to a homescreen redesign. Swiping down from the top left now brings up your notifications, while swiping from the top right instead shows a cover-screen-optimized version of the Quick Settings panel. Immediately, this feels more like a phone.
More exciting is what happens when you swipe up from the bottom: you get an app drawer. By default, this is populated with a selection of Samsung’s own apps that are optimized for the square screen, plus a “Labs” section with third-party options including Netflix and WhatsApp. But right below that, Samsung has included an easy prompt to install MultiStar, the Good Lock module that lets you run any app you’d like on the outer screen. 
Samsung used to bury the option deep in the phone’s settings, only to be found by those who knew to look for it. The bottom of the app drawer isn’t quite front and center, but it’s much more prominent than it used to be.
You can still run apps in three forms: full-screen, with the cameras blocking part of the software; a square display that stops just above the level of the cameras; or a thin portrait-aspect ratio that letterboxes the sides. A small virtual button at the bottom of the screen lets you cycle through them. 
Good performance isn’t guaranteed. Some apps, like Withings’ health tracker companion app, are almost impossible to use on the cover screen, with no configuration that leaves enough space for its graphs to fit. Google Maps is only a bit better — I love the idea of quickly checking my walking route without opening the phone, but there are so many floating interface elements that it’s unwieldy at best. Others work smoothly, but feel pointless: I can stream HBO Max on the tiny outer display, but I’d never want to.
But for other apps, the new cover screen options feel genuinely freeing. I can open Todoist and tick off a task, dip into WhatsApp to send a message, or open MyFitnessPal to log the snack I just ate. They’re quick actions that work well enough on the small screen, and because other apps — *cough* Instagram *cough* — don’t, I can dive into them without the risk of getting dragged into doomscrolling. That little bit of friction is just enough to save me from wasting 20 minutes I’ll never get back.
[Image: Like last year’s phone, the cover screen wraps around the cameras. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/samsung-galaxy-z-flip-8-review-07.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
As for the hardware, little has changed. The Z Flip 8 is 0.6mm thinner and 8g lighter than its predecessor. This is the thickest of Samsung’s three current foldables, but it’s more compact than Motorola’s Razrs, its only real rivals.
Samsung didn’t upgrade the Z Flip 8 with the thinner, tougher titanium display stack found in the two new Z Fold 8 phones, which also means this has just as visible a crease as ever. It rarely bothers me, and is hard to see head-on, but you may feel differently. The IP48 rating is a more objective issue, and means that while this phone is mostly safe from water, it’s still vulnerable to dust.
On the inside, you’ll find the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 if you’re in the US, though my UK model runs Samsung’s Exynos 2600. Exynos chips get a bad rep, but performance has been smooth so far, and I have no real complaints.
As with the Z Fold 8 phones, Samsung switched to more energy-dense silicon-carbon batteries for the Z Flip 8. Unlike those phones, it didn’t actually increase the battery capacity, but instead used smaller cells with the same 4,300mAh capacity — the key to shrinking the phone itself. Still, battery life is solid, reliably lasting the full day with battery to spare. The charging — 25W wired, 15W wireless — is relatively unimpressive, and the only way to get Qi2 charging is still by using a compatible magnetic case.
Storage and RAM remain the same as on the Z Flip 7; the screens do too apart from small bumps to peak brightness, and the cameras are also identical to last year’s. The 50-megapixel main camera is impressive, and especially helpful since the form factor means you can use it for selfies too. The 12-megapixel ultrawide and 10-megapixel inner camera aren’t remarkable, but they get the job done. A slab phone at this price would have better cameras, and most likely a telephoto lens, but the lenses here are good enough.
The question is whether it’s all good enough for the price, given Samsung has bumped the Z Flip 8 up to $1,199.99, a $100 increase. Z Flip 7 owners certainly shouldn’t upgrade, and anyone else should consider buying that phone instead, since the difference between the two is slight.
After all, the big upgrades are software, and unlikely to remain exclusive. Last year’s Z Flip 7 hasn’t yet been updated to One UI 9, but since its outer screen is almost identical, it seems likely to get the upgraded software, giving one less reason to opt for the new model. The Z Flip 6 and earlier, with their smaller cover screens, seem more likely to miss out. I’ve asked Samsung about its upgrade plans, but haven’t yet heard back.
Most of the other software upgrades aren’t even Flip-specific. Customizable, AI-powered cards have been added to the daily Now Brief; My FanCam lets you crop video to focus on a specific subject; and Audio Eraser can now dim background noise and highlight dialogue in apps like YouTube and Netflix. You’ll find those features across all of Samsung’s new foldables, plus the new Galaxy S26 FE.
Modest as the Z Flip 8’s hardware upgrades are, it feels like a turning point for Samsung, which is mostly done trying to limit the ways people use the cover screen. Given the speculation that the short, wide Z Fold 8 could replace the Flip form factor as Samsung’s “small phone that unfolds to a big phone,” it makes sense to close the gap between them.
The Z Fold 8 is a more capable phone than the Z Flip 8 when closed, its squat screen more usable than the Flip’s tiny one, despite Samsung’s software upgrades. But I have a real soft spot for the Flip form factor, which is tiny and pocketable when closed and a normal, almost compromise-free flagship phone when open — and endlessly satisfying to flip shut.
More than that, I enjoy its frictions. I welcome Samsung’s move to make it easier to use full apps on the cover screen, but I also welcome that it will never be entirely successful. Some apps simply don’t work on a screen this size, and the Z Flip 8 is all the better for it.
Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge
Agree to Continue: Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8
Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate.
To use the Galaxy Z Flip 8, you must agree to:
* Google Terms of Service
* Google Play Terms of Service
* Install apps and updates: “You agree this device may also automatically download and install updates and apps from Google, your carrier, and your device’s manufacturer, possibly using cellular data.”
* Samsung End User Licence Agreement
* Samsung Terms and Conditions
There’s also a variety of optional agreements, including:
* Provide anonymous location data for Google’s services
* “Allow apps and services to scan for Wi-Fi networks and nearby devices at any time, even when Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is off.”
* Send usage and diagnostic data to Google
* Google Gemini Apps Privacy Notice if you opt in to using Gemini Assistant
* Turn on Samsung offline finding
* Samsung news and special offers
* Bixby personal data intelligence
Other features, like Google Wallet, may require additional agreements.
Final tally: seven mandatory agreements and more than nine optional agreements.

articles.title: When Fruit Is Scarce, These Monkeys Hunt Animals
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/when-fruit-is-scarce-these-monkeys-hunt-animals-the-behavior-may-offer-clues-about-the-origins-of-humans-meat-eating-habits-180989412/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49489274
Points: 19
# Comments: 1
articles.body:
The bearded capuchins of northeastern Brazil typically eat plant-based foods, but they turn to small vertebrates when those sources are limited. Our ancestors may have done the same, eventually allowing predatory behaviors to be more frequently passed on in our lineage
Researchers observed bearded capuchins in Brazil eating birds (shown here), lizards, rodents, opossums, snakes and other small vertebrates.
The bearded capuchin monkeys of northeastern Brazil eat a mostly plant-based diet, chowing down on palm nuts and other fruits. But when plant foods are scarce, the primates consume a surprisingly diverse smorgasbord of small animals, including snakes, opossums, iguanas, bats, rodents and bird eggs and nestlings, researchers report in a study published on August 26 in the journal PLOS One.
The findings reveal new details about the diet and behavior of these highly adaptable, long-lived monkeys. But they could also shed light on the evolution of human diets, including our ancestors’ shift toward eating more meat.
Hunting small prey seems to help capuchins cope with seasonal fluctuations in plant food availability—and “this may have also been the case for hominins,” study co-author Susana Carvalho, a primatologist at Gorongosa National Park in Mozambique, tells Science News’ Jake Buehler.
Capuchins were observed eating birds (top left), marsupials (top right), lizards (bottom left) and snakes (bottom right).
S. Carvalho et al., PLOS One, 2026 under CC-BY 4.0
When the researchers started studying wild capuchins in the privately owned area of Fazenda Boa Vista roughly two decades ago, they primarily wanted to investigate the monkeys’ tool use and other complex behaviors. But while following two groups of the primates, scientists noticed that they were actively hunting and consuming small backbone-bearing creatures, or vertebrates—an intriguing behavior for a species that usually eats fruit. So, the researchers began making detailed notes whenever they saw the monkeys going after animals.
They ended up with more than 5,000 hours of observations between May 2006 and December 2010, recording 446 instances of capuchins eating animals. The team also looked at factors that may have affected the animals’ diets, including the age and sex of the individual monkeys that were chowing down on vertebrates, rainfall, temperature, humidity and the relative abundance of fruits and insects at the time.
The overlaps revealed some clear patterns. When plant foods became scarcer due to seasonal fluctuations, the monkeys seemed to hunt more. Lizards and rodents made up most of their prey, but the monkeys hunted a wide variety of animals. Scientists spotted males and females of all ages feasting on small vertebrates, but the behavior was more common among adult and juvenile males.
And when their hunts were successful, the monkeys seemed to go for the brains and guts first, before eating the rest of the body.
“This may allow them to obtain energy-rich fats and other nutrients quickly, which could be especially advantageous when prey is likely to be taken by another group member,” says study co-author Noemi Spagnoletti, a conservation biologist at Sapienza University of Rome, in an interview shared by the journal.
Did you know? Tool use
Among primatologists, bearded capuchins are famous for using stone tools to obtain food. They’ve been observed placing palm nuts on a hard surface and smashing them with rocks to reveal the tasty kernels inside. Wild females have also been seen using sticks or blades of grass to pick their noses and eat any boogers they extract.
Chimpanzees often get the limelight for eating vertebrates, but a range of nonhuman primates also engage in the behavior, Margaret Bryer, a biological anthropologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the study, tells Science News.
But while chimpanzees are some of our closest living relatives, bearded capuchins and humans are only distant cousins, and the creatures are not considered a direct model for our ancestors. However, the monkeys share enough similarities with humans that they might offer some clues about the evolution of early hominin behavior.
Humans are the only primates around today that regularly hunt animals larger than themselves—but how and why our ancestors evolved this behavior remains largely a mystery.
One hypothesis posits that our ancestors started eating smaller prey in times of seasonal plant food scarcity, before eventually leveling up to bigger game.
“As late Pliocene and early Pleistocene eastern African hominin environments became increasingly seasonally arid, the availability of plant-source foods that are key to many primates’ diet in forest habitats would have only been available intermittently, whereas animal resources would have remained accessible throughout the year,” the researchers write in the paper. “This may have selected for a higher frequency of predatory behaviors in our lineage.”
The new findings seem to support this possible explanation, suggesting that hunting small animals might have been a “stepping stone to the exploitation of larger prey” for humans, Carvalho says in a statement.
“The fossil record now needs re-analyzing to look at evidence of small vertebrate predation” by early humans, she adds.

articles.title: Mum of Nottingham attacks victim backs calls to stop killers' early release
articles.summary: Emma Webber has joined more than 30 families in signing an open letter to the government.
articles.body: Image caption, Emma Webber has joined more than 30 families affected by homicide calling for the change to the government's early release schemeBySonia KatariaEast MidlandsMore than 30 families have called on the government to stop killers convicted of any form of manslaughter being released early to ease prison overcrowding in England and Wales.In a letter to Justice Secretary Alex Norris, the families said they felt victims were "being asked to bear the consequences of the prison capacity crisis".Signatories include Emma Webber, whose son Barnaby was stabbed to death in the Nottingham attacks in 2023, and whose killer Valdo Calocane was convicted of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility.  Speaking on Radio 4's Today programme, Bridget Phillipson, Minister for Women and Equalities, defended the early release scheme.She said the government had faced "some really difficult and unpalatable choices" in dealing with prison overcrowding and that they had faced "the wholesale collapse of the criminal justice system".The scheme, external aims to ease prison overcrowding in England and Wales.The families of those affected by homicide have called for those convicted of any form of manslaughter to be excluded.Those convicted of murder and those serving sentences for rape, serious child sexual abuse and grooming offences are already excluded from the early release scheme.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Andrew Harper suffered fatal injuries while on duty in 2019Calocane fatally stabbed students Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, both 19, and school caretaker Ian Coates, 65, on the streets of Nottingham on the morning of 13 June.He then stole Coates's van and used it to drive into three other people, seriously injuring them.Calocane admitted three counts of manslaughter and three counts of attempted murder on the basis of diminished responsibility, and was sentenced to an indefinite hospital order in January 2024.The letter comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham indicated the government would make changes to the early release scheme to ensure that the killers of PC Andrew Harper, who were convicted of unlawful act manslaughter, are not eligible.The letter also highlighted concerns that some of the most serious domestic homicides result in convictions of voluntary manslaughter and that it would be "difficult to reconcile with the government's commitment to halve violence against women and girls" if those offenders were released early.Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Barnaby Webber, Grace O'Malley Kumar and Ian Coates were killed by Valdo Calocane in 2023The families said they had "deep concerns about how early release may apply in homicide".They wrote: "As the government considers excluding unlawful act manslaughter from the scheme, it must follow that all forms of manslaughter are also excluded."We have spoken with numerous bereaved families affected by homicide."A consistent theme has emerged: many feel that victims are being asked to bear the consequences of the prison capacity crisis through the earlier release of those convicted of the most serious offences."Whether intended or not, this is creating a growing sense that justice for victims and public protection are being compromised in order to address pressures elsewhere in the system."We therefore urge the government, as it seeks to prevent those responsible for the killing of PC Harper from benefiting from the early release scheme, to ensure that voluntary manslaughter is also brought within the proposed exemption."Other signatories include:John Hunt, whose wife Carol and their daughters Hannah and Louise were killed in their home by Louise's ex-boyfriend Kyle Clifford in 2024. Clifford was convicted of three counts of murder and sentenced to a whole-life order. Diana Parkes, whose daughter Joanna Simpson was killed by her estranged husband Robert Brown in 2010. Brown was convicted of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility.John and Penny Clough, the parents of Jane Clough, a nurse who was murdered in 2010.Josh Rook, whose sister Annabel Rook was murdered by her partner Clifton George in 2025.'Not isolated voices'Campaigners and victims' organisations have also backed the change.Frank Mullane, chief executive officer of Advocacy After Fatal Domestic Abuse, said: "The breadth of support for this letter demonstrates the strength of feeling among bereaved families."These are not isolated voices. Families from many homicide cases in recent years are united in calling for a clear and consistent approach to homicide and early release."Jo Early, chief executive officer of Support after Murder and Manslaughter, said: "Bereaved families understand the pressures facing the justice system."But they should never feel that justice for victims is being diluted because of those pressures. The most serious offences should be treated consistently and public confidence must be protected."Currently, 5,000 people are set to be released early, down from 6,000 after some exemptions were announced as part of an urgent review.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Bridget Phillipson spoke about the subject on Radio 4's Today programmePhillipson said: "We have been clear that the most serious offenders will be exempt from that early release programme. "But the reality of what we are confronting is that, if allowed to go unchecked, we could end up in a position where someone who is arrested for very serious offences, for example offences related to violence against a woman, and we wouldn't have anywhere to send that individual."A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: "We share the public's anger that these options are even being considered, after we inherited a prison system on the brink of collapse."We are fixing this by building 14,000 new prison places, expanding electronic tagging on an unprecedented scale, and investing in probation services at record levels."We are also exploring how we can go further, including faster deportation of foreign criminals, better use of the women's estate and reviewing the unjust IPP sentences."The prime minister has asked the justice secretary to present a plan for further changes of the early release scheme to parliament next month.Phillipson confirmed that "full details" would be set out before parliament next week.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in NottinghamMore on this storyRelated internet links

articles.title: Royal Navy warships track Russian vessels for three days in UK waters
articles.summary: HMS Duncan, HMS St Albans and HMS Severn used radars to monitor four vessels as they passed through the North Sea and English Channel last week.
articles.body: Royal Navy warships and a helicopter spent three days tracking Russian Navy vessels and sanctioned cargo ships in an "intense" operation in the North Sea and English Channel.HMS Duncan, HMS St Albans and HMS Severn used radars to monitor four vessels last week, while a Merlin helicopter provided surveillance from the sky."Since that successful operation, we have seen Russian shadow fleet vessels increasingly forced to change their routes, imposing significant cost and delays to their journeys," Gen Sir Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord and Chief of Naval Staff, said.It comes as data shows Royal Navy activity to monitor Russian movements is up 25% so far this year compared to 2025.During the August operation, the Royal Navy warships including a Type 45 destroyer and a Type 23 frigate, tracked Russian destroyer Admiral Levchenko as it escorted sanctioned cargo vessels General Skobelev and Sparta south through the North Sea and into the English Channel. The Royal Navy said Russia was "forced" to respond with "costly military resources" including the frigate Neustrashimy.A statement said a Nato ally then took over monitoring off the coast of France, without specifying the country.The operation comes after Royal Marine Commandos boarded a Russian "shadow fleet" oil tanker in the English Channel in June.Marines joined by National Crime Agency (NCA) officers, with the support of the RAF, intercepted and boarded the Smyrtos in a six-hour operation - the first of its kind by UK armed forces.NCA officers arrested an Indian national, 38, on suspicion of sanctions offences under the Russia Regulations and he was taken into custody.

articles.title: Musicians-turned-detectives are hunting for AI grifters
articles.summary: As audio-focused generative tools and platforms have gotten more sophisticated, the internet has become increasingly filled with AI-generated music whose melodies and vocals are algorithmically derived from the work of human artists. While some of the people pumping out this kind of content immediately own up to using AI, others have denied using the technology until increasing public scrutiny for
articles.body:
As audio-focused generative tools and platforms have gotten more sophisticated, the internet has become increasingly filled with AI-generated music whose melodies and vocals are algorithmically derived from the work of human artists. While some of the people pumping out this kind of content immediately own up to using AI, others have denied using the technology until increasing public scrutiny forced them to tell the truth. 
For musicians — especially those creating art in technologically-focused spaces like electronic dance music — the increasingly complicated question of what is “real” and what isn’t feels particularly urgent and personal. Professional courtesy can make this only more complex;  listeners can call out performers they suspect of using gen AI, but it’s something else for artists to raise concerns about their professional peers. There are some though, like 26-year-old EDM producer Max “H4RRIS” Harris, who are taking a stand against generative technology with videos calling out anyone they believe is trying to pass off AI slop as human-made art.
When I recently spoke with Harris, he told me that he sees AI-generated music as “a kind of decoy art form,” and he thinks that the people making it don’t really have anything meaningful to say with their creations. He feels that true art in any medium is “created by people that are trying to express feelings and messages,” and he believes that the only thing AI boosters are really interested in is making a quick profit.
“I don’t consider AI-generated material to be art, and I don’t think this technology is really advancing art in any meaningful way,” Harris said. “It’s a technological advancement that’s giving people a way to steal real art and pass it off as their own.”
Harris, originally from Maine, described his approach to making music as being fairly similar to working in other creative mediums. He always begins with a core concept before he starts “throwing more ideas down until I find something that sticks.” And as complicated as his workflow might look to someone unfamiliar with all of the tools and programs that he uses — his production setup includes Ableton Live, Novation Launchkey 49 MIDI controller, Ableton Push 3, Launchpad X, a couple of analog synthesizers, Serum, Diva, and the software sampler Kontakt — he said that the entire process is “really just me making creative decisions” that culminates in a sound that feels right.
“Each of those decisions — and there’s hundreds of them to go into each song — brings me closer to evoking a specific kind of idea or emotion,” Harris explained. “And then once I have a song mapped out, I have to start making even more choices about how to mix it in a way that makes it sound good and presentable.”
In Harris’ view, being a real artist means being able to make those kinds of experimental but informed creative decisions using your own studied understanding of a given medium. One of Harris’ biggest issues with gen AI is the way the technology often eliminates a user’s need to think about how songs (or books, films, podcasts, etc.) come together. But he has also been dismayed at the way that AI posers are muddying listeners’ understanding of what human-made EDM actually sounds like. 
“Aside from the similar vocals, you can usually hear a sharp hissing throughout the track,” Harris said of AI-generated songs. “I think that comes from the way that these models often work by starting with a big white noise block and then making guesses about waveforms by referencing data taken from real songs.”
Harris pointed to MANSA’s “Midnight on My Mind” and Danny and Ian Asher’s “Take Me (To The Moon)” as what he thinks are examples of AI-produced songs that embody what he jokingly refers to as “the AI revolution” that’s responsible for polluting the EDM space. MANSA, Danny, and Asher have not publicly commented on whether they use generative tools in their music. But Harris and other EDM fans have noticed the similarities between “Take Me (To The Moon)” and another person’s AI-generated track. There’s no definitive evidence that MANSA produced “Midnight on My Mind” with AI. Harris could very well be wrong about these songs being generated with AI. But his insistence that they are reflects the larger culture of mistrust that has developed in response to the growing presence of AI content online.
Harris holds AI production company Suno responsible for the recent spike in this kind of music being uploaded to the internet, but he also credits specific quirks of the platform for helping him learn how to spot songs worth calling out.
“Something I’ve noticed with a lot of Suno-generated tracks is that a lot of the time, you’ll hear the vocals and other melodic elements will start stuttering at the same exact time,” Harris explained. “These models still have a hard time fully separating different parts of the songs they’re trained on, and they treat these elements like one big instrument. As a music producer, all of these things come across like choices that a human just wouldn’t make with their compositions because it just doesn’t make sense.”
In some instances, the visuals accompanying AI tracks are part of what prompts Harris to accuse people of slinging AI. You might not be able to hear the generative models behind evangelical Christian AI persona Lionsaddle’s music, but you can clearly see the character’s fingers vanishing in and out of existence in videos. There is also an overly glossy visual quality to most of the videos posted by Christian house musician Midnite Manna that makes their content look a lot like what we typically refer to as AI slop.
Suno also came up multiple times during my conversation with 39-year-old Italian turntabilist-turned-producer Nihil Young. Young’s posts on Threads about people using Suno are what initially inspired Harris to make his videos. Like Harris, Young has spent the past few months watching multiple EDM newcomers’ stars rise after they post music he thinks was generated with AI tools like Suno’s. And while Young isn’t usually one to get involved with online discourse, he felt it was important to speak out about how many people are flooding the scene with AI tracks.
“These songs are the sound of Suno, which to me means that the people behind the songs are just straight up uploading original, copyrighted tracks of artists like Madonna and asking the platform to remix them,” Young told me, referring to Josh Fawaz’s “Like a Prayer” cover, which now includes AI credits following a wave of online backlash. “If they can do it with major artists like her, they can do it with you, me, and everyone else, which just isn’t cool. They can take your entire catalog, feed it to Suno, and generate ‘new’ songs from that stolen work.”
Young claimed that in response to his Threads posts, he received multiple hacking attempts and a wave of online harassment from AI defenders. He also told me that he thinks people bought fake followers to boost his Spotify numbers as a way of casting doubt on his authenticity. That spooked Young — who is raising a young daughter and just put out a new album of his own — to rethink whether he should continue. He’s taken a break from callouts, but he still thinks it’s important to know about the way AI music is harming human artists.
“Music production is where most of my income comes from, and almost as soon as AI began rolling out, I started losing many of my clients,” said Young, who has previously done audio mixing and mastering work for Sony Music, Warner, and Universal. “I can only imagine what it’s been like for singers, graphics artists, and people working in other creative fields. Whether you realize it or not, this stuff is impacting everyone.”
What Young wishes more listeners could appreciate is how easy it has become to generate entire songs with platforms like Suno. In his opinion, most people using AI to make music “aren’t actually doing anything creative and they don’t have a true artistic process” because many generative tools on the market involve some degree of autogeneration. When I brought up how detailed AI prompts can be, he insisted that many of the people posting AI music likely aren’t even writing their own inputs. Young noted that Suno’s Simple Mode allows users to whip up songs by simply selecting a musical genre and clicking a button — a process that requires basically zero thinking. (Suno has not responded to a request for comment in time for publication.)
As much as traditional artists might loathe generative production, there is no denying that AI songs are making their way into the mainstream. In 2024, Metro Boomin took shots at Drake with a beat sampling comedian King Willonius’ “BBL Drizzy” — an AI track whose vocals, melodies, and instrumental elements were generated by AI music startup Udio. Metro Boomin’s “BBL Drizzy” went viral after the producer posted the beat to SoundCloud and invited other performers to rap over it. Drake subsequently rapped over the beat himself on Sexyy Red’s  “U My Everything,” and that song managed to peak at 44 on the Billboard Hot 100. 
Wholly AI-generated songs (and people) are finding success, as well. Last summer, Vinih Pray’s Suno-created song “A Million Colors” also peaked at 44 on TikTok’s Viral 50 chart, and AI artists Breaking Rust and Cain Walker made it onto Billboard’s Country Digital Song sales chart — a lesser-known chart focusing on individual song downloads. Meanwhile, Hallwood Media — a label founded by former Geffen Records president Neil Jacobson — signed AI avatar Xania Monet to a $3 million recording deal. Certain segments of the industry are clearly trying to normalize AI-generated music, and people are definitely making money with their machine-generated tracks. Kapwing estimates that the top 10 most followed / streamed AI music creators on Spotify and YouTube collectively raked in over $6 million in 2025. And with platforms like Deezer reporting that AI songs now account for over 50 percent of new uploads, that kind of music is getting harder for listeners to avoid — if they can even recognize it. While streaming platforms are beginning to more clearly label AI songs, many listeners have reported that they can’t really hear the difference between generative and human-made music.
Aside from the people uploading all of these songs, no one has a way of being absolutely certain whether the tracks were generated with AI or made by an actual artist. AI music detection tools are one potential solution, but it’s not entirely clear how and, perhaps more importantly, if listeners might incorporate them into their lives. Judging by the numbers (which, of course, can be manipulated with paid streams), there do seem to be people who don’t mind the sounds of Suno and other AI tools. Young knows that most people’s ears probably aren’t well-attuned to identifying audio slop, but he still thinks that music lovers owe it to themselves to make the effort to find real, human artists.
“In my opinion, it becomes obvious that you’re listening to AI-generated music when you put on a good pair of headphones,” Young told me. “But I also think that a lot of people these days are consuming music like fast food and listening to it through the speakers on their phone. Or they just have it on a background noise, and they don’t necessarily care what it sounds like.”
