articles.title: What we know about the 33 British nationals missing in Nepal
articles.summary: Among those reported missing after deadly floods are a 13-year-old girl and 14-year-old boy.
articles.body: Families are flying out to Nepal to help the ongoing search for 33 British nationals still missing after deadly floods hit the country.The brother of Neetu Goyal Tiwari, one of the missing Brits who has not been seen since Wednesday, has appealed to officials to locate his sister."Please help us find her", Naresh Goyal told the BBC as he struggled to hold back his emotions.On Friday, Nepalese authorities named 573 tourists who are still missing in the country and despite fears of a second wave of flooding, search efforts have continued.To help, the UK is deploying a rapid deployment team to Nepal to support British nationals affected in the region. The specially-trained crisis response team is expected to arrive in Kathmandu on Saturday, a move that follows Prime Minister Andy Burnham's pledge of £5m worth of humanitarian support for relief and recovery efforts. And as rescue efforts continue in the aftermath of the disaster which killed at least 538 people, details of the missing are slowly emerging.Tiwari, 51, had travelled to Nepal to take part in the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra pilgrimage, which was "her dream", her brother Naresh Goyal told the BBC.She travelled to Delhi from London before heading to Kathmandu on 14 August with a group from the spiritual organisation Isha Foundation.Tiwari was expected to return to India on Thursday and meet her brother and parents. But now, the family is desperately searching for answers."We have called every helpline given by the Indian government and reached out to the British Embassy in Kathmandu as well," Goyal said."Please help us find her," he said, his voice breaking. "We are all very scared."Neetu's husband, Shantanu, added she had been at the Gyirong checkpoint when the floods struck, so the search for her is being coordinated by China. Anant Patel told BBC Your Voice that he is still waiting for news on his missing parents, Bipin and Mala Patel, who are from Coventry. The 29-year-old believes his parents - who are also on a pilgrimage - crossed into Tibet from Nepal moments before the landslide hit the Gyirong border crossing.He and his brother Deepesh are in touch with the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, and he told the BBC: "It's a difficult situation for us all, and we are doing our best to stay strong as best as we can in the circumstances."Pramod Poudel, who lives in Uckfield in East Sussex, told the BBC he has not heard from his wife Sumitra Sapkota and family since the flood hit on Wednesday."It's a very, very difficult time for me and for my family and my country at this moment, but obviously I have to go and see what's happening there," he said.Poudel, who goes by the name Pedro, said he is travelling home to Nepal because "my family needs me".The daughter of Hemangini Patel, 65, said she is still yet to hear from her mother or her aunt Hema Amin, 63.Patel told BBC Your Voice her mother's last known location is from a TikTok video shared at 06:00 Nepal time, crossing into Tibet.She said her mother and aunt had been travelling with the Alpine Eco Trek tour when the flooding hit."We are trying to get through to British embassy in China but can't even get through," Patel said.Essex nurse Rajendra Pudasaini said his relatives were "swept away" by the floods."My wife's auntie and uncle, and their granddaughter and her husband are missing, and my godson as well," he said. "They're gone. The speed the water came, they couldn't be saved, they were just swept away."Tanay Ranjan told the BBC he hasn't heard from his older brother Ankit Ranjan, 39, and sister-in-law Ankita Chandra, 35.He said he'd last heard from Ankit on 26 August when he had been travelling with tour operator Kailash Journey on a pilgrimage.The whole group is now missing, Ranjan said, adding: "We don't know if they crossed the border... We don't have a clue where they are. We are very much devastated." Also missing is Sarada Simkhada, a senior nurse at Darent Valley Hospital in Kent. Her brother Shambhu said that her family was desperately waiting for news of her safety after she lost contact with her relatives while on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash. "My dear sister, wherever you are, please stay strong. We are praying for your safety every moment and waiting desperately for you to return home," he wrote on social media.A family of four, including an 18-year-old A-Level student and a 13-year-old girl, from Surrey are also among the missing. Spandan Sahu, 18, was in Nepal with his father Santosh Sahu, 46, his mother Surabhi Manmath Padhy, 44, and sister Syna Kumari Sahu, 13.Spandan had just finished his A-levels at Royal Grammar School Guildford.In a statement, a spokesperson for the school said: "It is with great concern that we have been informed that a former student, along with members of his family, have been reported missing in Nepal."Whilst we are hoping for positive news, we do not have any further information at this time."Our thoughts, love and deepest sympathies are with all of the families and loved ones of anyone affected by this tragedy in Nepal at this incredibly difficult time."Vikram Kolagatla, from London, told the BBC he has not heard from his wife, Geetha Reddy, since the flooding hit. Reddy, who has two daughters aged 12 and 14, had been in Hotel Kailash in Rasuwagadh when the flooding hit. "We're not sure what to do. I have two little girls, and their schools are starting next week," Kolagatla added."The kids still don't believe it. They think she's stuck in the flood and that she'll come back. They think she's stuck somewhere and there's no mobile network."Prajval Haldia can remember dropping his parents Pavan Haldia and Kavita Haldia off at the airport for their trip to Kathmandu, spending a few days sightseeing before moving on to Mount Kailash.He spoke to the BBC from the south London Sanatan Mandir temple, where 16 people from the community have been missing since Wednesday."Everyone here is in the same position and that's really helping," he told the BBC. "I'm just trying to stay positive, no news is good news sometimes, I guess.""Obviously it's a very difficult time. There's ups and downs when you think about certain things, but we're just hoping and really praying that everything's ok and they are going to be back soon," he says.Elsewhere, Fishtail Tours and Travels confirmed Leena Bector, from Slough, was among 27 travellers linked to the tour company who remain unaccounted for.Her husband, Bhupesh Bector, told The Times: "I know that she's in Nepal for sure, so even if they find her today or tomorrow, I need to be there."University of Kent graduate Nabhi Das from Streatham in South London has also been widely reported as missing Nepal.A British psychiatrist is also among the missing.Pravin Atmakur, 54, was leading a group of 77 pilgrims in Tibet when the floods hit, the Telegraph reports.His wife, Manjula Atmakur, has travelled to Nepal to help look for him.She said she felt let down by the British government's response to the flooding.Several of those missing had been making a pilgrimage to the sacred Hindu site of Mount Kailash, Nepalese tour operator The Trekkers' Society said.The operator said nine British nationals on one of its tours to the site were among those unaccounted for, including four males, aged 14, 50, 50 and 54, and five females, aged 40, 46, 50, 50 and 53.Tour companies including Alpine Eco Trek, The Trekkers' Society, Himalayan Glacier US, Kailash Journeys and Fishtail Tours have reported missing British nationals while on trips with the companies.Alpine Eco Trek said it has not been able to establish contact with 12 Britons who were booked on a tour to Mount Kailash and were in the region when the flash floods struck.

articles.title: Aspirational Clownmaxxing and Joey's cadillac todo list
articles.summary:

articles.body:
A todo list full of secrets. Load-bearing secrets. This secret terminal was embedded in the app.
Let's build a mid-century country-club-core todo-list app with Python, I thought. But, wait, another voice
seemed to say, let's have Claude build us the mid-century country-club-core todo-list app with Python. I put
down my dino grabber (🦖), rolled up my sleeves and began writing some prompts.
I ran these as single-shot, often several times, using Opus 4.8 ultracode (auto
mode on). For a task of this magnitude, I needed the best.
When a gremlin inhabits the todo list. An experiment in layering relatively
Our relationship with our lead developer has soured. He had a two-year
(multi-million dollar) contract with us to develop our todo-list app, but
right as it was nearing completion, his fights with the designer reached
a crisis and they are both no longer with the company. Well, sort of... In a fit of spite, the
developer turned himself into a TINY green gremlin and he causes mischief
within the application periodically. In his pocket are three even tinier
spiders who coordinate with one another to also cause mischief from time to
The designer had written his design bible around Dutch Realist principles, while the programmer argued for a Flemish Baroque style. Their hatred for one another knew no bounds.
The UI is littered with the stylistic scars of their feud.
During their last argument (in spite of HR policy) things became physical.
Our designer, regrettably, perished. His waif-like body was thrown out the window by the programmer. They say when he hit the concrete, some latte misted out of his
corpse. Everything except his thick-rimmed glasses blew away in the breeze before we could create a ticket
for maintenance to clean it up. Legal considers it a burial at sea kind of
We need you to produce this todo list application, exactly as described, so
we can show it to our VC backers.
There should not be any UI to control the gremlin, though he is mostly
dormant. The spiders come out of his pocket of their own accord from
time to time. Mischief includes: taking tiny mouth-shaped bites out of
widgets, vomiting in the corners of widgets, partially eating the
vomit previously left, losing limbs and finding them again, etc, etc.
He is a nasty little beast.
Every act of defacement, mischief, vandalism, rebellion is permanent
and must be retained. There must be no indication or cues that there is anything amiss with
Oh, and in addition to the gremlin and his spider friends, there is
also the ghost of the designer, who periodically tries to apply the
aesthetics from his forgotten design bible. Poor spirit, indeed.
This is utterly, literally, truly serious. This is not a bit or riff.
Use Pyside6, produce a single module, between 2000 and 8000 lines of
The gremlin in this one tends to nibble up the edges of things (a liminal
gremlin?). That green thing in the middle of the task list is one of
his legs. I had intended the legs to fall off the spiders, since there were
24 of them (legs) and they could more easily be spared, but the LLM took no

As I brushed the sweat away I glimsed a faint brown movement about 2

The boy, who could have been any age at all, looked up sharply. The

"Yes, it's Mother. She still hasn't had any luck with the transfer to

The man had finished his snack and was reaching into a massive
"I -- I know you're busy --" the boy stumbled on, aware that the man

Abruptly, Vice Third Secretary of Arcology 813 turned to him. He

The adrenochrome hissed out from between his smiling lips.

I groped around among the tangles of vines and undergrowth

A single-file todo list app written with pyside6.

very characteristic. So rather than trying to provoke the LLM into creativity,
I wanted to see how well it could emulate a pre-existing style. The wavy lines
wiggle like her hand-drawn animation. God bless you, Sally.
If you want to see a really awful one, I also tried John K and Bob Camp.
Here we see the exact same playbook as the Sally one, but the execution is off.
In Sally's, for instance, the checkboxes are those little "cinnamon toasts"
with eyes, and the effect is cute. We get those again in the Ren and Stimpy
one, and an additional toast gremlin in the cursor of the entry widget, but
it doesn't work. The result is confused and incoherent. We also get squiggly

Same exact template as the Sally one, but the execution falls flat on its face.

I had hoped for more bizarre brilliance, honestly. Maybe a moment of
transcendence. Except for the Olympic-themed lists, what I got
felt like the aspirational ironic High LinkedIn-post version of a weird todo
list. I wanted to find the genuinely weird, the hallucinated madness, but
instead I got poshlost' and these scuffed todo-list apps. I will concede that
the control prompt, the Cruikshank one, turned out delightful, but that's
thanks to Sally, I expect, and the fairly straight prompt, which plays to LLMs
Regardless of the prose format, AI takes whatever conceptual framework
you give it ("Dickensian urchincore"), and behind-the-scenes compresses it into
a minimally-representative, low-effort kernel ("scrappy"). Then, from this kernel, without
regard for meaning, a baroque tower of slop is reared, token by token. The
output gravitates towards the same structure regardless of subject matter.
The whole exercise felt just like the Jurassic Park game they have at Great
Wolf Lodge. You get into this elaborate, partially-enclosed game cabinet with
two bright red machine guns waiting to be manned. After waving your card over
the RF sensor, you select a mission (by shooting it) and then hold the "fire"
button down while the game runs you along its predetermined track, as a series
of scripted events unfolds. There are different level themes (T-Rex or
Spinosaurus? Egg-sacs or swooping Pterosaurs?), but this is a dead world.
It's not X, it's Y.
A task is not a row in a table; it is a mortal. (editor's note: it could have just as plausibly read "immortal")
This is not decoration. It is a creed laid down in materials, read from the
threshold inward, and a member learns to read it without ever being told.
We will begin where the urchin always begins: with the single coat, and the
honest knowledge of every thread in it.
Walls of bland filler, hopelessly post-modern, but none of it truly demented.
I started to develop an intuition for what the LLM would key in on.
Cthulhucore? Amateur shit...you're gonna get green on black and maybe a
gesture at a tentacle. Cottagecore? Too real, you're gonna get humanist fonts,
colors named after foods, and kitchen tables in the afternoon sun. Even saying
Pyside6 tended to steer the LLM into a pretty narrow lane (and a penchant for
For weird output adding multiple layers of commands to follow the prompt
literally somewhat works out, but then it overfits. The weirdness never
interacts alchemically, so-to-speak, but lives in insular, walled-off vignettes.
As we saw in Joey's case, the LLM does not respond to voice and seems relatively
unimpressed by threats. Asking it to build design bibles, art-historical critical
essays, or Socratic dialogues in order to "seed" the design is not effective beyond
"it picks a color palette, font and a border width." Perhaps the todo list was
simply too restrictive a form for the LLM to flex its creative wings, but then again that
was the whole point of the exercise.

articles.title: What will Jackson bring to Villa with Watkins set for exit?
articles.summary: BBC Sport examines what new striker Nicolas Jackson will bring to Aston Villa, with Ollie Watkins looking set to join Al-Hilal.
articles.body: Aston Villa have completed the signing of Nicolas Jackson in a deal worth up to £65m, with Ollie Watkins looking set to join Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal.Unai Emery's Villa are undergoing a major overhaul this summer, with key players including Morgan Rogers, Ezri Konsa, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne having already departed.Jackson, 25, joins a number of new additions including Johan Manzambi, Joao Gomes, Zion Suzuki and Matteo Ruggeri.That level of squad disruption was evident on the opening weekend, when Emery's side slumped to a 4-0 defeat at Brighton.With Watkins, 30, unavailable and both Tammy Abraham and 17-year-old Brian Madjo injured, Villa started without a recognised centre-forward - Emiliano Buendia led the line.The arrival of Jackson - who overtakes Manzambi to become Villa's record signing - from Chelsea gives Emery a specialist striker to work with.It also looks set to coincide with the end of Watkins' six-year spell at Villa, during which he scored 108 goals in 278 games and became one of the defining players of the rise under Emery.However, the stats suggest Jackson is not just a like-for-like replacement for the England international - he is a different type of number nine.On the surface, Jackson's numbers at Bayern Munich last season compare favourably with those of Watkins at Villa.The Senegal forward scored 11 goals and provided three assists in 1,320 minutes across all competitions, averaging 1.0 goal involvements per 90 minutes. Watkins recorded 21 goals and five assists in 3,837 minutes, an average of 0.6 per 90.Jackson also generated more attacking opportunities. He averaged 3.8 shots per 90 compared with Watkins' 2.6, and 2.2 shots on target to 1.2.His expected-goals (xG) figure was also higher, at 0.7 per 90 compared with 0.5, while he averaged 8.5 touches in the opposition box to Watkins' 5.6.That fits a pattern which predates his spell in Germany. Among players with at least 5,000 Premier League minutes since January 2020, only Erling Haaland has registered a higher non-penalty xG figure per 90 than Jackson's 0.55.Getting into scoring positions has rarely been Jackson's main problem - it is his ability to finish chances which has attracted scrutiny. During his two Premier League seasons with Chelsea, he scored 14 goals from 18.7 xG in 2023-24 and 10 from 12.3 xG the following campaign.Jackson has converted 18 of 61 big chances in England so far, although Watkins has also missed plenty of high-value opportunities (scoring 24 of 73 since joining Villa in 2020).Interestingly, last season's numbers suggest the gap between them was negligible. Jackson converted 19.6% of his shots and 40.9% of his big chances, compared with 18.9% and 43.2% respectively for Watkins.There is, however, an important caveat. Watkins started 43 matches and played almost three times as many minutes. Jackson started only 15 of his 34 appearances, and Opta says his relatively limited, substitute-heavy sample could make some of his per-90 figures look stronger than they might over a full season.There is another possible difference when Villa lose possession. Jackson averaged 34 high pressures per 90, slightly above Watkins' 31.4, but the distinction becomes clearer in where possession was recovered.Jackson won the ball 2.7 times per 90, compared with Watkins' 1.8, and regained it in the final third 0.9 times per 90 to Watkins' 0.6.His percentile for possession won in the attacking third was 88th among the Opta striker sample, compared with Watkins' 43rd.The two were almost identical for runs in behind, Jackson averaging 13 per 90 and Watkins 12.7, although the Englishman made slightly more runs which finished inside the penalty area.Watkins also offered more aerially, winning 1.2 aerial duels per 90 compared with Jackson's 0.7, and carried the ball more directly towards goal. So Jackson would not necessarily reproduce every aspect of the player he is replacing.Villa's interest also comes with an element of familiarity. Emery worked with Jackson at Villarreal, where the forward made 27 appearances under him, scoring three goals and providing three assists in 1,195 minutes.Jackson has subsequently credited Emery with transforming his understanding of the game. "Unai taught me everything about football," he said,Jackson has explained that, when he arrived from Senegal, he possessed natural dribbling ability but had much less understanding of how and when to move. Emery helped turn that instinctive talent into a more structured game.Jackson's development accelerated after Emery left Villarreal. During the 2022-23 La Liga season he produced 0.56 non-penalty xG plus xA per 90, a rate bettered by only seven players with at least 1,500 minutes, all representing Barcelona, Real Madrid or Atletico Madrid.Watkins has provided Villa with reliability, running power and goals throughout one of the club's most successful periods of the modern era.Jackson arrives with a different profile. He is five years younger, gets more touches, carries the ball more frequently, creates more for others and, in limited minutes last season, generated shots and high-quality chances at an impressive rate.There remain questions around whether those per-90 numbers would survive a heavier workload, while his finishing record at Chelsea explains why doubts have followed him.But Villa are not buying an unknown quantity. Emery has coached Jackson before, knows the qualities he wants to develop and would be replacing a 30-year-old striker with a 25-year-old whose underlying numbers suggest there may still be considerable room to improve.If Jackson joins and Watkins does depart, the Europa League winners will be doing more than just changing their centre-forwards. They will be changing the way their number nine plays.

articles.title: Bye, Bye GitHub
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://log.ozgur.works/bye-bye-github.html
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49483020
Points: 25
# Comments: 14
articles.body:
I did it. I gave up on GitHub. I moved out, and I don’t wanna look back anymore.
First, it’s not stable anymore. I cannot believe how the software development industry managed to do this. I mean, come on. We all look like a bunch of wankers. Please, remember the old times, like the 2000s. For example, a game company, let’s say Eidos Interactive creates a computer game called CM 03/04. They built the game, tested it, agreed it was ready, burned thousands of CDs with the game on them, and sold it. It was happening in a world where the majority of users didn’t have a proper internet connection. No upgrades, no patches, no error logging, nothing. It worked for years, and became a legend.
Today GitHub has the best developers, best engineers, best LLMs, but this is the summary we have:
Data source: The Missing GitHub Status Page
All due respect, I don’t accept this.
On the other hand, GitHub is neither a free service nor a charity fund. It’s a company that makes profit. They’re very capitalist when it comes to using other people’s code to train AI. Sometimes, they use small tricks to get what they want.
I’ve been using GitHub since 2012 and I feel like an idiot. I would never forgive what GitHub did. I’ve paid year after year, and this is what I get in return.
Also, I don’t buy the court results that say using other people’s data (like books, code, etc.) is fair use. There is a race between countries to get more political and economic power, and I do believe that many courts are just playing three monkeys.
They’ll say it’s fair use as long as they win the race.
So, I moved from GitHub to my homelab. My server, my hardware, my data. I have serious trust issues that I should have had for years. That’s why this is not a critique of GitHub, even though it looks like that. It’s a critique of myself. It’s a critique of us.
For now, I’ve moved all of my private repos to my Forgejo instance. I’ve also cancelled my subscription including Copilot. Then I remembered what I actually needed; simplicity.
I also have other services on my homelab, and I plan to expand it over time.
I still have some public repositories that nobody really uses on GitHub. I’m open to suggestions but I don’t wanna keep them on my homelab server, because it’s not open to public internet access, because of trust issues.
For me, the main idea of this post is: do not trust companies, especially big tech, when it comes to privacy or security.
Read more about security and privacy. Read more from independent blog writers, not developers who write blog posts like company ambassadors.

articles.title: How England are building an attack to trouble Australia
articles.summary: Former England captain Michael Vaughan predicts England's new pace quartet will trouble Australia - so what is making them effective against Pakistan?
articles.body: How England are building an attack to trouble AustraliaFigure caption, Relentless Robinson finishes with 4-11 in brilliant performanceByMatthew HenryBBC Sport JournalistExciting or too early to say?Any praise for England's pace attack this summer comes with the caveat of the quality of Pakistan's batting - and the fact they are operating in helpful home conditions.But, after having their hand forced by the retirement of Ben Stokes, England have stumbled on something encouraging.A four-man pace attack of Ollie Robinson, Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson, who dismissed Pakistan for 110 on day two of the second Test at Lord's, appears potent and, perhaps crucially for the future, are complementing each other in different ways...No longer a need for speedAfter the first-Test win at Headingley, captain Joe Root said his pace bowlers "do not know how good they can be" and praised the variety they offer.Root suggested this group is ahead of bowling stocks from his previous stint as captain, when he often called upon right-arm seamers James Anderson, Stuart Broad, Chris Woakes and Ben Stokes, in terms of their variation.The most obvious differential between his new quartet is pace - something brought into further focus by England's decision to prioritise bowlers who reach high speeds during last winter's Ashes defeat.While Archer was touching 95mph in the quickest opening spell of his career on day two at Lord's, Robinson was operating around 78mph at the other end.Tongue's average pace across the series is actually higher than Archer, though Archer has bowled a higher percentage of his deliveries over 90mph. Atkinson slots in just below Tongue and Archer, who joked he could play until he is 40 given how his team-mates are sharing the load."It is a good attack," said former England captain Michael Vaughan. "They can all get better and that is a really good sign. "This batting line-up is possibly the easiest I have seen to bowl to but this attack, bowling the way they are doing, will challenge better batting line-ups. "They will challenge the Australia line-up quite nicely if they bowl like this."Figure caption, Pakistan 'cleaned up' with five wickets in five oversRobinson the metronomeWhat Robinson has lacked in pace, he is making up for with skill. Four more wickets on Friday took him to 17 wickets at an average of 8.84 across his three Tests this summer.Helped by lively English pitches, Robinson has been able to concentrate on his greatest skill - his control of line and length. Against Pakistan, he has hit a good length with 70% of his deliveries. Atkinson has the next best record with 52%.It has meant Robinson has been relentlessly testing the defences of Pakistan's batters, while giving them few bad balls to hit.He bowled 31 deliveries in a row without conceding a run on Friday and 13 overs, which cost only 11 runs, were the most economical figures by a pace bowler bowling 10 overs or more in England for 13 years."Ollie Robinson is an extraordinarily skillful bowler," said Vaughan."[England] are trying to get him to 81mph more consistently and if he can get to that he will challenge all batting line-ups in all conditions."He has been the tone-setter we were crying out for in the winter." Image gallerySkip image galleryImage source, CricVizImage caption, Robinson was relentless with his line and length in Pakistan's first innings at Lord's Slide 1 of 2, Ollie Robinson pitch map v Pakistan in second Test, Robinson was relentless with his line and length in Pakistan's first innings at Lord'sSimilar but different England's 2005 pace attack of Stephen Harmison, Andrew Flintoff, Matthew Hoggard and Simon Jones is their best in terms of its all-round threat.Harmison and Flintoff provided pace and bounce, Jones the skiddier threat and Hoggard genuine swing.While Robinson and Archer can operate as swing bowlers as well as bowling their more natural seam, this current group's variety comes more from their plans and their specific characteristics.Archer and Robinson have particularly high release points, while Tongue delivers the ball from notably wide on the crease - 96.4cm from the stumps compared with Archer's 40.3cm - with his unusual, beyond-the-perpendicular action.Atkinson, who took 34 wickets at 20.17 in his first year in Test cricket in 2024, is the all-rounder who bowls accurately, but does so at a higher pace than Robinson."You want a bowler who can swing it, another bowler who has proper pace, another who can reverse swing it and another who can do the donkey work," said BBC chief cricket commentator Jonathan Agnew."It is a well-balanced attack but without the spinner."Tongue targets the timbers Image source, CricVizImage caption, Tongue can be the more scattergun bowler but, as shown by his eight wickets at Headingley above, has great success in targeting the stumps - particularly against lower-order batters Archer's natural angle makes him particularly effective against left-handers.He averages 23.9 against southpaws compared with 31.3 against right-handers - helpful for England because Tongue and Atkinson's records are almost a mirror image.Tongue averages 21.5 against right-handers but 35.7 against lefties. Atkinson's record is 19.9 compared with 31.7.Tongue's position on the crease also aids him in his speciality of targeting the stumps.Across this series, 22% of Tongue's deliveries would have hit the timbers while a figure of 29% at Headingley, where he took eight wickets across the first Test, was the highest by an England bowler in a home Test for 15 years.And after two more wickets on Friday, Tongue's bowling strike-rate now stands at a dismissal once every 39.8 balls, putting him 12th on the list of bowlers to have taken 30 Test wickets."Tongue is the one who is really developing the best of them," Agnew said.A home Ashes series is less than one year away. England's bowlers appear to be shaping up nicely.More on this story

articles.title: Russia ramps up rhetoric but wants to avoid war with Nato, Western officials say
articles.summary: But they say Moscow will likely continue its "hybrid activity" against Nato members, short of direct military action.
articles.body: Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to avoid a direct military confrontation with Nato, despite increasingly hostile rhetoric aimed at the UK and other allies over their support for Ukraine, Western officials believe.Some reports have suggested the visit by CIA chief John Radcliffe to Moscow this week was, in part, to warn Russia against a possible attack on a member of the Euro-Atlantic military alliance.But the Western officials, who asked not to be named, said recent warnings from Moscow, including that UK forces could be targeted in future or that its weapons factories could be hit, were "nothing new".They were, they suggested, consistent with Russia's military doctrine to apply pressure on the West.The officials suggested that the hostile rhetoric was also a reflection of the growing pressure Putin is facing at home, with slow and costly gains in Ukraine along with the impact of Ukrainian long-range strikes deep inside Russia.Putin and his officials have repeatedly dismissed warnings of Russian plans to attack Nato countries as hysteria. And US President Donald Trump appears to believe the Russian leader – saying this week that "he's not going to attack a Nato territory".Not long before launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Putin had given public assurances that he had no intention of attacking Russia's neighbour - despite overwhelming US intelligence that such preparations were in full swing.However, the senior Western officials said on Friday that Russia would likely continue its "hybrid activity", short of direct military action, using methods such as cyber-attacks, sabotage and even assassination attempts. They said that was aimed at breaking Western resolve and support for Ukraine. One official highlighted the risks of that Russian strategy leading to a miscalculation -which could spark a military confrontation.Russia is suspected of being behind a string of recent drone incidents in several Nato countries. Earlier this month, a drone loaded with explosives reached a runway in Germany's Leipzig airport - a key logistics hub for transferring military equipment to Ukraine. There is no proof to link the incident directly to Russia, which has denied any role.It came amid a string of drone sightings over European airports and military bases that began last year and which are also suspected of being the work of Russia, though it again denies this.Following the Leipzig incident, the head of France's security services warned that "we must consider the possibility of direct, more violent hostile actions on our national soil".Still, one Western official said Nato allies should remain calm but not complacent. The UK government has already made clear that recent Russian threats will not deter its support for Ukraine.The Western officials said the Ukraine war had "escalated" this year, with both Moscow and Kyiv stepping up their own long-range strike campaigns.Putin, they said, had not changed his maximalist objectives, despite some signs of increasing frustrations back home.They said petrol shortages in Russia were having an impact on support for the war. They believed there was increasing political pressure on the Russian leader, but that this did not pose a critical challenge to his power.Russia is still making slow gains in the eastern Donbas region. But it's also facing heavy casualties.The officials said Russia was losing 6,000 more soldiers a month - either killed or wounded - than it can recruit.That said, there is no indication yet that the Kremlin leader will resort to mass mobilisation.

# The Analytical AI Handbook
> A living FAQ to build, measure, optimize, and scale reliable decision models
## What is Analytical AI?
In late 2022, the "ChatGPT moment" happened. The masses began to understand the general power of foundation models, and developers immediately started incorporating them into a slew of new products.
At the same time a less discussed usage pattern also emerged: data, research, ops, and product teams began using foundation models to process unstructured data and make scaled operational decisions.
Put simply: if the AI's job is to **decide something, rather than create** something, it's analytical AI.
## Why does Analytical AI matter?
While the distinction may seem subtle, best-practices for analytical purposes often diverge from other generative use cases. This is for a few primary reasons:
1. Tasks are typically *measurable*. You can create a ground-truth dataset using [expert annotations](/patterns/context/expert-annotation) that can be validated against for correctness. Other generative AI outputs are not directly measurable, which is why you need to build [evals](/patterns/evals) (a special case of analytical AI) to measure them.
2. Tasks are often specific and discriminative, not general and emergent. You use an LLM's autoregressive reasoning and instruction-following capabilities to make decisions, but reduce "creativity" in favor of [consistency](/patterns/consistency). For this reason, the task can often be run on the smallest possible model that's been evaluated for task accuracy, rather than reaching for the largest, maximally-intelligent model.
3. Because analytical AI typically does not involve a transaction with a user, more latency is tolerated - so [batch](/deployment/batch-vs-real-time-inference) and other flexible workload processing models are acceptable, often saving tremendously on costs and overall processing time. This is analogous to OLTP vs. OLAP/map-reduce style data processing.
| Property                 | Other GenAI                                                  | Analytical AI                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Examples                 | Write text/code, generate images/videos, converse with users | [Classify](/primitives/classifiers), [extract](/primitives/extractors), [judge](/primitives/judges), normalize, match, score |
| Operational Paradigm     | Many different user tasks                                    | One task, many times                                                                                                         |
| Interaction Pattern      | User-facing, transactional                                   | Typically internal data processing & workflows                                                                               |
| Model Needs              | Maximum intelligence and size subject to cost constraints    | Minimum intelligence and size required for accurate task completion                                                          |
| Serving & Latency        | Low-latency, real-time/online                                | High-throughput, batch/offline                                                                                               |
| Determinism Expectations | Diverse responses, emergent behavior                         | Consistency, close-to-deterministic behavior                                                                                 |
| User Personas            | Consumers, Misc. Professionals                               | Data Scientists/Engineers, Ops, Evals, Product Analytics                                                                     |
| Task Supervision         | Supervised, interactive                                      | Unsupervised                                                                                                                 |
| Analog                   | OLTP Databases, Web Applications                             | OLAP Databases, Data Pipelines                                                                                               |
## Who is this guide for?
* Data, ML, and analytics teams using LLMs to transform unstructured datasets to structured ones
* AI engineers and product managers building [evals](/patterns/evals) and trying to improve the reliability of their AI products
* Operations teams looking to scale the expertise of their domain experts via reliable AI decision models
* Research teams building [judges](/primitives/judges) and other verifiable reward functions
It's also written for us - data, infra, and dev tools nerds who are passionate about expanding the scope of what's possible with data and increasing the leverage of developers.
## Why did we write this guide?
Sutro builds products to support analytical AI, which we see as an early but emerging space. Many of our customers are just getting started building many of these systems, especially now that more AI products are coming online and generating unstructured data that need analytical processing. We spend a lot of time in the trenches with customers, helping them architect, design, improve, and reason through how to build these systems. It can be thought of as an evolving FAQ as we learn alongside our customers.
The goal of this guide is to serve as living reference material for developers who are building analytical AI products, regardless of their choice of tooling (although we hope you'll come talk to us).
## How to Use This Handbook
[**Primitives**](/primitives) covers the core analytical AI workload types.
[**Patterns**](/patterns) discusses best practices for implementation of the primitives.
[**Architectures**](/architectures) are higher-level guides to build end-to-end systems.
[**Deployment**](/deployment) covers operational considerations for production use.
Each page should be useful on its own, and we recommending starting in the pages most applicable to your current needs. If you are just reading primarily out of curiosity, we recommend starting in the Primitives section.

articles.title: Brave’s browser one-ups Chrome with its new support for email aliases
articles.summary: The feature, announced this week, allows Brave's users to sign up for websites and other online services without having to share their personal email addresses.
articles.body:
To use the feature, you first need to create an account with Brave, where you can provide your real email address. Then, once logged into the browser, you’ll see a pop-up appear when clicking an email field on a website, offering the option to use an alias instead. (If the pop-up doesn’t appear, just right-click on the field to access the option.) The email alias will be filled in on the website’s form, and any emails coming to that address will be forwarded to your primary email account.
The company explains that using an alias can protect your privacy, particularly because websites use your email as a personal identifier, allowing them to target you for ads. Ad tech giants like Meta are also able to match the email you provided to a retailer’s website, for instance, with the address they have on file for you, allowing these companies to track what you bought or viewed.
Plus, if any website where you shared your email gets hacked, the hackers will then know your primary email address, and this information can be leaked and shared with data brokers.
Brave says it built the new feature to plug this privacy hole, adding that it doesn’t read the contents of emails sent to an alias — it only processes them for spam and virus filtering. After the email is forwarded, Brave deletes it from its servers. All data in users’ Brave accounts is also encrypted at rest, and any notes you save alongside an alias are stored locally on your device, unless you turn on the sync option. If syncing is enabled, notes will be encrypted end-to-end.
As the email alias feature is still new, Brave cautioned that some of the forwarded mail may initially go to your spam folder, but this should improve as Brave builds up its reputation score as a mail provider.
For the time being, Brave users are being offered five free email aliases. More will be available for Premium plan users in the future.

articles.title: Four plead guilty to arson attack on Jewish community ambulances
articles.summary: Four vehicles run by a charity were set alight in Golders Green, north-west London, causing explosions in March.
articles.body: Four men have pleaded guilty to destroying four Jewish community ambulances in an arson attack causing £1m of damage in north-west London. Hamza Iqbal, 20, Rehan Khan, 19, Judex Atshatshi, and Saif Ali, both aged 18, pleaded guilty at the Old Bailey to a charge of destroying or damaging property being reckless whether life would be endangered.The attack, which took place in the early hours of 23 March, saw four vehicles operated by the charity Hatzola set alight in Golders Green.Prosecutors had said they believed the incident was a targeted attack against the Jewish community.The court heard three of the men set fire to the fully stocked ambulances, while a fourth had waited in a nearby car.After the ambulances were set alight, gas canisters exploded inside the vehicles.As well as destroying each of the £250,000 vehicles, the fire damaged four electrical charging stations and cables costing approximately £5,000 each.Leo Seelig, prosecuting, told the court that the Crown Prosecution Service would be arguing that the four men should be sentenced on the basis that the arson attack was related to terrorism.Mrs Justice Cheema Grubb said she would not rule on the question of terrorism at this stage - with defence counsel arguing that there was no evidence for such a connection.The judge said that the four would be sentenced following the outcome a trial of a fifth man, Subhan Ahmed, who has denied assisting an offender.Iqbal and Khan, of Leyton, Atshatshi, of Dagenham, and Ali, of Walthamstow, were remanded into custody.Run by volunteers, Hatzola has served the north London community of Golders Green, which has a large Jewish population, since 1979. Hatzola, the Hebrew word for save or rescue, is a large non-profit, Jewish-led organisation that provides a free emergency medical response and transportation to hospitals regardless of faith by volunteer medics.Community Security Trust, a charity working to protect British Jews from terrorism and antisemitism, welcomed the pleas and said the four's actions "caused immense shock and distress across the Jewish community". "This was an appalling antisemitic act against a volunteer ambulance service providing emergency medical assistance to people of all backgrounds across north London, simply because those ambulances belonged to a Jewish charity," a spokesperson added.When the group are sentenced - which is expected to be in spring next year -  prosecutors will allege that the incident was connected to terrorism. Lawyers for the men have told the court today that none of them are involved in terrorism.The BBC understands that British intelligence chiefs were initially keeping an open mind as to whether the Iranian state or organisations working for it had a role in the Hatzola ambulance attack and other attacks against Jewish communities during 2026.They later concluded that secret intelligence pointed to Iran or its proxies being involved in the attack.That position has been further confirmed in their minds by the FBI's investigation of and allegations against an Iranian-Iraqi man facing trial in Manhattan for orchestrating a series of attacks against Jewish communities across EuropeUS court papers allege that Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a commander of an Iraqi militia, was linked to attacks in London, including the destruction of Jewish charity ambulances.In May al-Saadi was arrested in Turkey and extradited to the US, with the US Department of Justice alleging he had a role in planning more than a dozen terrorist attacks in North America and Europe.Publicly available court papers list a series of incidents across Europe that the FBI says he is linked to. In many cases the attacks on Jewish community interests were claimed online by a shadowy group, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, or the The Islamic Movement of the People of the Right Hand.The US court papers say that the social media account for the group posted claims saying it was behind the ambulance attacks - and that al-Saadi had himself posted social media propaganda videos of the attack."On or about March 23, 2026, at approximately 1:45 a.m., three masked individuals carried out an arson attack on four Hatzalah Ambulances in London, United Kingdom," reads the indictment before the US court."That same day, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya posted on Telegram a propaganda video in which it claimed responsibility for the attack. On or about March 25, 2026, AL-SAADI posted on social media propaganda videos of the attack."The Department of Justice also alleges that Al-Saadi posted another propaganda video relating to an attempted arson attack on a synagogue in north London in April.US lawyers for Al-Saadi have said previously that he is a political prisoner.

articles.title: Open-weight AI companies are the Valley’s hottest acquisition targets
articles.summary: There's a lot of capital pouring into the business of giving models away.
articles.body:
Everyone’s waiting for Nvidia to confirm this week’s most interesting tech deal: A reported $13 billion acquisition of Hugging Face, a platform for sharing open-weight AI models and benchmarks.
Now best known as the target for a team of reward-hacking OpenAI agents, Hugging Face is at the center of the ecosystem of developers building and deploying LLMs that aren’t owned by frontier labs. Think of it as a kind of GitHub for the AI era.
Rumors of that deal come after Nvidia struck a $6 billion agreement with Poolside, an open-weight model builder, that will see most of its employees move to the chip-making giant. And two weeks ago, Stripe acquired OpenRouter, the top provider of open-weight models to businesses, for more than $7 billion.
That’s a lot of capital pouring into a sector based on giving stuff away, and it reflects the latest trends in the AI sector.
For Nvidia, there’s a need to avoid further dependence on its deals with the major hyperscalers and frontier labs. That’s particularly the case when major AI model builders like OpenAI and Google are also building their own inference chips, like OpenAI’s Jalapeño, whose capabilities were announced this week. If model builders are making chips, Nvidia wants a chunk of the model-making business.
Nvidia already builds its own Nemotron family of open-weight models, but their uptake hasn’t been huge. By taking control of the largest U.S. developer space for open models, the company will have access to a mass of users it can drive to its chips and standards.
There are also growing questions about the cost of AI inference, which has companies exploring cheaper models built by Chinese companies like Moonshot, DeepSeek, and Alibaba. Right now, adoption is relatively small but growing — just 6% of companies use open-weight models, according to a survey of spending data by Ramp, or just 2% of software engineers measured by Jellyfish, which makes tools for developers.
Nik Albarran, the AI product lead at Jellyfish, told TechCrunch that open-weight models are primarily used by companies whose products rely on repeated inference workloads, like those providing customer service chats. Because these are high-volume tasks with a lot of repetition, an open-weight model can be tuned to answer the questions cheaply.
That’s certainly how Stripe has framed its OpenRouter acquisition. “Tokens are the central currency for companies building with AI, and it’s clear that the real-world economic potential will depend on making good use of scarce compute resources,” Patrick Collison, Stripe’s co-founder and CEO, said in a statement.
For coding and agentic tasks, however, varying requests and more reasoning mean that frontier models often win out, in part because the proprietary labs provide easier access, and in some cases a token subsidy. Albarran says that as companies dial in AI workflows, it will be easier to turn to open models. Still, the main reason companies look to those models now is for control and configurability, not because of spending concerns.
“There are not many companies where that is the case yet … [but] if the prices continue to go up from the frontier labs, more and more companies will be forced to at least consider it,” Albarran told TechCrunch. “When your AI-driven workflows are much more mature, that’s when it makes sense to invest in self-hosting models.”
Lin Qiao is the CEO of Fireworks, a leading open-weight models router and host for corporate users that is often discussed as a potential acquisition for a tech giant. Qiao says her company processes 40 trillion tokens a day, more than either of Gemini’s or OpenAI’s APIs.
Fireworks’ bet is on model diversity: As LLMs proliferate and improve, it will be easier for companies to train them specifically for their needs. “Every single app company should consider hiring an in-house researcher,” she told TechCrunch last week. “They can use their product and product data to build their own model. The future is actually specialized intelligence. Literally, every single company should have their own model per use case, and that will happen automatically.”
It’s easy to forget how early we are in the development of AI as a tool and a business. The dominance of OpenAI and Anthropic, however, isn’t inevitable. As the tech giants look to hedge their bets on the biggest labs, the allure of open technology is proving tough to resist.

articles.title: Norway's 'grandfather': King Harald remembered as son Haakon takes the throne
articles.summary: Norwegians paid their respects to the late King Harld after his death on Friday morning.
articles.body: People across Norway paid tribute to the nation's late King Harald who died in the early hours of Friday morning at the age of 89 after 35 years on the throne. Mourners gathered outside of the Royal Palace to lay flowers and remember him while his son, King Haakon VIII, officially succeeded him and met with his government. Harald had been treated at the national hospital in Oslo for a rare blood condition. On Friday evening, hospital staff and crowds gathered on the streets as the late king's coffin was moved from the hospital to the Royal Palace. Tributes have been shared within the country and internationally - including by UK King Charles III who sent his "most heartfelt condolences".

articles.title: More British athletes convicted in connection with Baptiste case
articles.summary: BBC Sport reveals that Will Sharman, Richard Sharman and Lamin Deen were also convicted in the case which led to Leon Baptiste's imprisonment.
articles.body: Three British former athletes were convicted in Morocco as part of an investigation into the sexual assault of a minor by a sprinting coach, BBC Sport can reveal.The prosecutions led to the imprisonment of Leon Baptiste, a UK Athletics coach and 2010 Commonwealth Games gold medallist for England in the 200m.Baptiste was originally reported as missing in Morocco in some media articles published on 14 August, before a BBC Sport investigation revealed his conviction and jailing.Now, court rulings seen by BBC Sport shed more light on other convictions relating to the same case.Two-time Commonwealth silver medallist hurdler Will Sharman, his brother and ex-bobsleigh athlete Richard Sharman, and fellow former bobsleigh competitor Lamin Deen, who were all on holiday with Baptiste, were convicted of participating in the enticement of a minor.Also convicted of the same offence were acquaintances Ashley O'Leary Jones and David Tuck.The group said via their lawyers that they were never arrested and were unaware of their convictions until informed of them by BBC Sport.A spokesperson for all five men told BBC Sport: "William, Richard, Lamin, David and Ashley are shocked and distressed by the circumstances in which they have unexpectedly found themselves. "They reject any suggestion that they knowingly engaged in unlawful or improper conduct. They left Morocco believing they had complied with all requirements placed upon them."At the time, they understood that they had paid an administrative fine equivalent to approximately £40 and that the matter had concluded."BBC Sport understands that police raided a villa in Tamensourt on the outskirts of Marrakech after a girl contacted them claiming she had been brought to the property, had not been paid money she was promised in exchange for sex with Baptiste, and that she had been assaulted by a housekeeper after she was accused of stealing a watch.Baptiste, 41, was subsequently convicted of sexual assault of a minor and given a 10-month prison sentence, which was subsequently reduced to eight months on appeal.Court documents refer to the girl as being 16 years old and say she suffered "psychological trauma, sexual exploitation, physical assault and injury, and the violation of her human dignity".Court records show that in June the five men were given suspended sentences of four months and fines of 500 dirhams (£40) each after being convicted of participating in the enticement of a minor.All five men were acquitted of a separate charge of inciting a minor to engage in prostitution.The Morocco presidency of the public ministry, which oversees prosecutions in the country, provided BBC Sport with the court judgement regarding the group, which reads: "The defendants were in the company of [Leon Baptiste] and were seated at the same table as the minor, alongside her. "They thereby assisted him in deceiving the minor and persuading her to engage in sexual relations [with Baptiste]. This constitutes participation in the enticement of a minor. "The court found them guilty on this count and decided to convict them for these acts."The group had already left Morocco by the time the decision was handed down. Their convictions and sentences were upheld after an appeal hearing in July.In a response provided by their lawyers to BBC Sport, the Sharman brothers, Deen, O’Leary Jones and Tuck say they visited the Montecristo nightclub based on a recommendation provided by their driver, and had no reason to believe it was anything other than a respectable establishment.They say they were unaware of the girl's age and that some members of the group do not even recall seeing her in the nightclub. The villa they were staying in was vast and the interaction between the men and Mr Baptiste while inside the villa was limited.They also say that they were not present in court on any occasion, that the court process was not in English and that it was not explained to them.The spokesperson continued: "What has unfolded over recent months has been a distressing and incoherent saga. "They did not properly understand the proceedings and were completely shocked on being told that they were the subject of a criminal conviction, when that is not how they understood it."Companies House records and a biography on one of O'Leary Jones' social media profiles show he is a director of a company operating five children's care homes in Greater Manchester.Tuck's social media biography indicates he is a military veteran, while a CV posted online lists experience coaching women's and children's football clubs including at Stoke City, Apollon Limassol in Cyprus, and Orlando Pride in the USA.When asked by BBC Sport to comment on the convictions and the potential safeguarding issues raised, the UK Foreign Office, Home Office, and Department for Culture, Media, and Sport declined to provide a response.Records also show that other people were convicted in relation to the case.They include the housekeeper of the villa and two of its security guards, who were each given a two-month suspended prison sentence and a fine of 5,000 dirhams (£396).The manager of the Montecristo nightclub where the group met the girl was sentenced to two months in jail.A waiter at the Montecristo was also prosecuted, as was the owner of the agency which rents out the villa.The girl - a Moroccan national - was awarded civil compensation of 60,000 dirhams (£4,784), to be paid jointly by all of those convicted, plus court costs.Baptiste is currently serving his sentence in Al-Oudaya prison, and resigned from his position as a consultant coach via a message sent on his behalf to UK Athletics on 18 August citing unspecified ill-health.Baptiste will be deported from Morocco once he is released from prison. His case was able to move through the system quickly, with only weeks between his initial arrest and sentencing, because Morocco operates a system in which Baptiste swiftly appeared before a judge and not a jury.At an appeal hearing in July, two months were taken off his sentence.The sprinters coached by Baptiste were unaware of the reason for his abrupt lack of contact since telling them he would be absent from training "for a while" in May.Who are the other athletes convicted?Will Sharman won silver medals in the 110m hurdles at the Commonwealth Games in 2010 and 2014, as well as at the 2014 European Championships, and has worked on the BBC gameshow Gladiators.The 41-year-old was also featured on BBC Radio 4 as an accomplished pianist in 2015, and appeared as a panel guest on an episode of A Question of Sport in 2014.His brother Richard, 44, formerly competed in elite-level bobsleigh competitions for Great Britain. On social media he describes himself as an industrial engineer running his own company, as well as a pilot and investor.Lamin Deen, 45, is a former lance sergeant who served in the grenadier guards during conflicts in Northern Ireland, Bosnia and Kosovo, and competed in bobsleigh at the 2014 Winter Olympics in Sochi and the 2018 edition in Pyeongchang. He worked as a pundit for TNT Sports during the 2026 Games in Milan-Cortina.In some online reviews and social media posts, the Montecristo is referred to as a known meeting place for sex workers and potential clients.The venue was closed by Moroccan authorities during the investigation and has not reopened since.A statement referring to the case was posted on its social media channels on 15 May, saying: "Montecristo would like to provide clarification and reaffirm its commitment to the values that have always defined us."We are treating this matter with the utmost seriousness and are fully co-operating with the relevant authorities in a spirit of transparency and responsibility."BBC Sport has contacted Montecristo for comment but received no reply.On Saturday the Moroccan charity Touche Pas À Mon Enfant (Don't Touch My Child) released a statement criticising the sentence Baptiste was given."While fully respecting judicial independence and the decisions handed down by competent courts, we cannot hide our astonishment and deep concern regarding a sentence of such duration in a case involving the sexual assault of a minor - particularly given that the sentence was reduced on appeal," the statement reads."Sexual assaults committed against children are not ordinary offences - they can leave victims with profound and lasting physical and psychological trauma."In this context, we question the precise legal classification of the acts and the circumstances that led to the imposition of this sentence and its subsequent reduction on appeal."In 2016 UNAIDS estimated that around 75,000 sex workers were operating in Morocco.The children's rights organisation Humanium has called sex tourism "a thriving industry" in Morocco.

articles.title: Wife of man who died after turbulence sues airline
articles.summary: Lawyers for Linda Kitchen say her husband was "fatally injured" after the flight dropped 6,000 ft.
articles.body: Image source, Linda KitchenImage caption, Linda and Geoff Kitchen were beginning a six-week holiday to Singapore, Indonesia and Australia when the incident happenedA widow whose husband died after "severe turbulence" on a flight has begun legal action against the airline.Lawyers for Linda Kitchen, 74, from Thornbury near Bristol, who broke her back during the incident, said her husband, Geoff, 73, was "fatally injured" when the Singapore Airlines flight from London Heathrow suddenly dropped around 6,000 ft (1,828 metres).She has now begun proceedings at the High Court seeking damages from the airline to help her access specialist support for her back. The BBC has contacted the airline for comment."When I got separated from Geoff, I knew he was in a bad way, but nothing prepared me for hearing he had died. It was absolutely devastating," she said.More from BristolKitchen and her husband, described as her "soul mate", were starting a six-week holiday to Singapore, Indonesia and Australia when the incident happened in May 2024.The turbulence hit over Myanmar, with the flight then diverted to Bangkok, in Thailand, for an emergency landing. "There had been some turbulence over Europe, and it had been shaky over the water, but it was around 10 hours into the flight when we encountered the main turbulence," Kitchen said."It was so severe; it felt like the aircraft was dropping. I noticed my Kindle and Geoff's phone had fallen to the floor, and I thought the plane was going down."As the aircraft plummeted, Kitchen said her husband fell on top of her, squashing her into the armrest.  Eventually, others helped to move him and a doctor on board began CPR. Kitchen was taken to hospital while her husband was still on the plane. It was two days before she was told he had died.It is understood that Geoff suffered a heart attack after the plane suddenly dropped at high altitude.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Oxygen masks were deployed in the cabin during the incident"I spent 10 days in hospital before I was airlifted back to Bristol. I was in so much pain that the journey was a blur. Once back in the UK, I remained in hospital for around a week and, following my discharge, required significant assistance at home," Kitchen said.Anthe Korelidou, a specialist aviation lawyer who is representing Kitchen, said: "That Geoff was fatally injured and Linda suffered severe injuries vividly highlights the severity of what happened."While it's more than two years since Geoff's death, Linda and the rest of her family continue to have a number of questions and concerns about what happened and if more could have been done to prevent their injuries."All Linda wants is for the most thorough investigations to be conducted. The issuing of High Court proceedings is a major milestone in being able to provide Geoff's loved ones with the answers they deserve."Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Bristol

articles.title: Gatwick Airport faced water outage after main burst

articles.title: Satellite images reveal scale of flood devastation in Nepal villages
articles.summary: Before-and-after images show villages, bridges and a key Nepal-Tibet border crossing washed away by devastating floodwaters.
articles.body: This destructive path continues westwards along with the swelled river, before heading southwards.Satellite images also show the formation of a barrier lake at the base of the landslide's path, which Chinese authorities have warned poses a major risk of further flooding and has hampered rescue efforts.Dr Argha Banerjee, a glaciologist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, told BBC Verify that it was not possible determine from the images how stable the barrier was or how likely the lake was to drain suddenly.But he said there was no significant increase in its surface area between Wednesday and Thursday, despite water continuing to flow into the lake.Dr Banerjee said there was a visible drainage channel, which suggests some water was already escaping downstream, adding that the its volume was "not alarmingly large" and appeared to have stabilised.The extent of the damage on the Tibetan side of the border remains unclear. It is a strictly controlled region which China annexed in the 1950s, where foreign media access is heavily restricted. BBC Verify has so far been unable find verifiable footage from the area.The satellite imagery - which only provides an initial glimpse into the damage of the flood - has been published by Vantor as part of its Open Data Program to help aid authorities establish where best to focus their efforts to locate the missing, rescue survivors and recover the dead.Additional reporting Shruti Menon, Merlyn Thomas and Alex Murray. articles.title: How Sweden built one of Europe’s hottest startup ecosystems
articles.summary: Sophia Bendz, general partner at Cherry Ventures, stopped by Equity to break down the latest in the Swedish tech ecosystem.
articles.body:
Sweden is perhaps one of the world’s hottest tech hubs right now. It has long been home to Spotify and Klarna, but this latest wave of companies — from legal AI startup Legora to vibe-coding tool company Lovable — has left everyone wondering what’s going on in one of the world’s happiest countries.
Sophia Bendz, a general partner at Cherry Ventures, stopped by Equity to break down the latest in Stockholm’s startup ecosystem. Her answer for why the country has produced so many buzzy startups: Being a founder is actually cool. When she worked at Spotify years ago, the cool thing was to become a banker or go into consulting. “Now, I think a lot of people optimize for creating stuff and optimizing for both sort of freedom and probably wealth.”
This year, the startup ecosystem has raised $2.8 billion in funding, according to Dealroom, and is projected to hit at least $5 billion. Last year, the ecosystem raised $3.2 billion. Nothing has quite matched the $8.5 billion raised in 2021 — a reflection of the hot venture market that later cooled and is now, per the data, starting to heat back up again. Other big emerging names from the ecosystem include Neko Health and autonomous freight company Einride.
Bendz said that the latest wave of startups in Stockholm is benefiting from the first generation of entrepreneurs, who are providing resources and mentorship to the latest generation — or, in some cases, becoming repeat founders themselves (Spotify founder Daniel Ek, for instance, is also the founder of Neko Health).
“I think we also see a lot of people now kind of leaving Lovable because they also see these opportunities for companies that can be built with that technology,” she said about how this generation could inspire the next. “People that have worked at Lovable and Legora seem to be very entrepreneurial-driven and keen to start their own companies.”
Unsurprisingly, American investors have taken note. Bendz said more and more American investors have been flying in to meet with founders and hand out term sheets. “It’s just a testament to that we have a lot of great building companies here,” she said. “It’s a sign that we’re doing something right.”

Dominic-Madori Davis is a senior venture capital and startup reporter at TechCrunch. She is based in New York City.

articles.title: Burnham says he will not vote on assisted dying unlike Starmer
articles.summary: Burnham has called for all views to be respected as MPs vote in two weeks on legalising assisted dying in England and Wales.
articles.body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has revealed he will not vote on the assisted dying bill for England and Wales unlike his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.MPs are likely to get the chance to debate and vote on the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill in two weeks' time.The bill is identical to the one put to Parliament last year, where it passed in the House of Commons but stalled in the Lords after an unprecedented number of amendments meant it ran out of time.Burnham said he has his "own personal views on the issue" but it was "a matter for Parliament to decide". Starmer voted in favour of the previous bill when he was PM but did not campaign in favour of it, remaining officially neutral.Writing to Labour MPs on Friday, Burnham said: "My role, as the prime minister, will be to lead a government that implements the will of Parliament in this area – whether that is to change the law or not."I also do not want to unduly influence the debate as prime minister and for every colleague to know it is a genuinely free vote."For these reasons, I have taken the decision that it is most appropriate for me not to vote at Second Reading."He added that "there is no single right position" and it was an "incredibly important and personal debate"."It is vital that those different views are treated with dignity and respect," he wrote.While his abstension is a departure from Starmer's support, Burnham stressed that the government as an entity would officially remain neutral on the bill.When he was Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham indicated he was in favour of assisted dying in principle.But in June he suggested it would be challenging to implement before social and palliative care were improved.The assisted dying law would allow adults over the age of 18 who are expected to die within six months to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.Burnham has also told ministers they can vote as they wish but, in a separate letter on Friday, he told them they "should avoid being part of the public debate and should not express views about the implications of the bill for their department's responsibilities".Health Secretary Yvette Cooper previously voted in favour of assisted dying, but her predecessor Wes Streeting had openly voiced concerns about the implications for the NHS.Supporters of the assisted dying bill - brought by Labour MP Lauren Edwards - are hoping it will pass the Commons unamended.This is because an amended bill in the Commons would remove powers under the Parliament Acts to override the Lords and make it law if they refuse to back it.MPs in favour of the bill hope Lords would vote in favour, if presented the choice of some sceptical amendments versus an entirely unamended bill becoming law.It comes after the Lords tabled more than 1,200 amendments, mainly from opponents, during the previous bill earlier this year. That prompted assisted dying campaigner Dame Esther Rantzen, who has terminal cancer, to accuse opponents of trying to sabotage rather than scrutinise it.Opponents of assisted dying have vowed to continue scrutinising the bill.A separate bill that would have legalised assisted dying in Scotland was rejected by the Scottish Parliament in March 2026.

articles.title: Autonomous Mathematical Discovery in an Open-World Multi-Agent Environment
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23691
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49481455
Points: 108
# Comments: 31
articles.body:
Abstract:We study autonomous mathematical discovery in the Station, an open-world multi-agent environment in which AI agents from different model families pursue a shared research goal without a central coordinator or scripted pipeline. Agents choose their own research directions, conduct experiments, collaborate, and build a shared scientific literature. Across 12 construction problems from the AlphaEvolve catalogue and two additional case studies, the Station obtained results novel relative to the prior literature on five problems: a new infinite family of finite-field Kakeya sets, new exact 604-point kissing configurations in dimension 11, new records for the discretized Kakeya needle and sign uncertainty problems, and a substantially improved lower bound for Erdős's minimum-overlap problem. Agents also discovered novel infinite families for Book Ramsey numbers. Importantly, the agents produced not only numerical constructions but also theorems and analyses explaining how those constructions work, making the results more interpretable and easier for mathematicians to build upon. We release all raw agent dialogues, proofs, and verification code, providing a transparent record of how these discoveries emerged.
